title: 10  Session 8 — Exploratory Data Analysis and Visualization
text:
11.1 1. The first pass
Exploratory Data Analysis is the deliberate look at a dataset before modelling it — to understand what is there, to find problems, and to form the questions worth asking.






Tip🧠 Analogy — the doctor’s examination



A doctor does not begin with surgery. They take a pulse, listen to the chest, ask questions. Most of it finds nothing — and that is the point. The examination rules things out, and occasionally finds something that changes the plan entirely.
Skipping EDA is operating without examining. It works right up until it does not.


Five questions, asked in this order, on every new dataset:








#
Question
Tool




1
How big is it, and what type is each column?
.shape, .info()


2
What does each column look like on its own?
histogram, box plot, .value_counts()


3
What is missing or impossible?
.isna().sum(), .describe()


4
Which columns move together?
scatter plot, correlation


5
What differs between groups?
groupby, pivot table




11.1.1 The dataset for this chapter
datasets/city_homes.csv — 500 properties across three cities, with 25 areas unrecorded, because real files have gaps.

import numpy as np, pandas as pd

homes = pd.read_csv("datasets/city_homes.csv")

print(f"1. SHAPE — {homes.shape[0]} rows, {homes.shape[1]} columns\n")
homes.info()
print("\n3. MISSING VALUES per column:")
print(homes.isna().sum())

title: 10  Session 8 — Exploratory Data Analysis and Visualization
text:
12.1 2. Matplotlib in one page
Matplotlib is Python’s base plotting library. Almost every chart follows the same four steps.



Step
Code




1. Make a figure and axes
fig, ax = plt.subplots()


2. Draw something on the axes
ax.hist(...), ax.scatter(...)


3. Label it
ax.set_xlabel(...), ax.set_title(...)


4. Show it
plt.show()




12.1.1 Demo 1 — the four steps

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.2))          # 1. create
ax.hist(homes["price"] / 1e6, bins=40)            # 2. draw
ax.set_xlabel("Price (₹ millions)")               # 3. label
ax.set_ylabel("Number of houses")
ax.set_title("How much do these houses cost?")
plt.show()                                        # 4. show







Figure 12.1: A histogram of house prices. Steps: create, draw, label, show.





Note the title. It is a question, not a label. "Price distribution" tells the reader nothing they could not see; "How much do these houses cost?" tells them what to look for.
crumbs: 10  Session 8 — Exploratory Data Analysis and Visualization

title: 10  Session 8 — Exploratory Data Analysis and Visualization
text:
12.2 3. Choosing the chart
The chart follows from the question and the column types — it is not a matter of taste.








Your question
Column types
Chart




How is one number spread out?
1 numeric
histogram


What is its centre, spread and outliers?
1 numeric
box plot


How many of each category?
1 categorical
bar chart


Do these two numbers move together?
2 numeric
scatter plot


Does this number differ by group?
1 numeric + 1 categorical
box plot by group


How do all my numeric columns relate?
many numeric
heatmap


How does something change over time?
time + numeric
line chart









Warning⚠️ The pie chart is almost always the wrong answer



People compare angles badly. Any pie chart with more than three slices is harder to read than the bar chart of the same data — and a bar chart can be sorted, which a pie cannot. Use a bar chart.



12.2.1 Demo 2 — histogram versus box plot: what each one hides

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.2))
ax[0].hist(homes["price"] / 1e6, bins=40)
ax[0].set_title("Histogram — shows the shape"); ax[0].set_xlabel("₹ millions")
ax[1].boxplot(homes["price"] / 1e6, orientation="horizontal")
ax[1].set_title("Box plot — shows the summary"); ax[1].set_xlabel("₹ millions")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

q1, med, q3 = homes["price"].quantile([.25, .5, .75])
iqr = q3 - q1
flagged = ((homes["price"] < q1 - 1.5*iqr) | (homes["price"] > q3 + 1.5*iqr)).sum()
print(f"skewness {homes['price'].skew():.2f}  →  the histogram shows a right lean")
print(f"the box plot flags {flagged} houses as outliers by the IQR rule")
print("The histogram cannot tell you that count; the box plot cannot show you the shape.")







Figure 12.2: Same column, two views. The histogram shows the shape; the box plot shows the summary and flags outliers.





skewness 0.59  →  the histogram shows a right lean
the box plot flags 0 houses as outliers by the IQR rule
The histogram cannot tell you that count; the box plot cannot show you the shape.




12.2.2 Demo 3 — bar charts for categories

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

counts = homes["city"].value_counts()
means  = homes.groupby("city")["price"].mean().sort_values(ascending=False) / 1e6

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.2))
ax[0].bar(counts.index, counts.values)
ax[0].set_title("How many houses per city?"); ax[0].set_ylabel("count")
ax[1].bar(means.index, means.values, color="darkorange")
ax[1].set_title("What does a house cost per city?"); ax[1].set_ylabel("₹ millions")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(counts.to_string())







Figure 12.3: Counts, and the average price per city. Two different questions, two different bars.





city
Mumbai    207
Pune      172
Nagpur    121


Two bar charts of the same column that answer completely different questions. The left one is about how the data was collected; the right one is about houses.

12.3 4. Seaborn: statistical charts in one line
Seaborn sits on top of matplotlib and knows about DataFrames. What takes six lines in matplotlib usually takes one in seaborn.

12.3.1 Demo 4 — grouped box plots, which is where seaborn earns its place

import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.4))
sns.boxplot(data=homes, x="city", y="price", ax=ax[0])
ax[0].set_title("Does price differ by city?")
sns.violinplot(data=homes, x="bedrooms", y="price", ax=ax[1])
ax[1].set_title("Does price differ by bedroom count?")
for a in ax: a.set_ylabel("Price (₹)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(homes.groupby("city")["price"].agg(["count", "median"]).round(0))







Figure 12.4: Price by city, and by number of bedrooms. One line each.





        count     median
city                    
Mumbai    207  6994000.0
Nagpur    121  1413000.0
Pune      172  2944500.0


A violin plot is a box plot with the distribution’s shape drawn on it. Use it when the shape matters — for instance when a group is secretly two groups.

title: 10  Session 8 — Exploratory Data Analysis and Visualization
text:
13.1 5. Scatter plots
A scatter plot puts one column on each axis and one dot per row. It is the fastest way to see whether two numbers are related, and what kind of relationship it is.

13.1.1 Demo 5 — four relationships, four shapes

import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt

import pandas as pd

rel = pd.read_csv("datasets/four_relationships.csv")
x = rel["x"].values
pairs = {
    "Strong positive": rel["strong_positive"].values,
    "Weak positive":   rel["weak_positive"].values,
    "Curved":          rel["curved"].values,
    "No relationship": rel["unrelated"].values,
}

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(13, 3))
for ax, (name, y) in zip(axes, pairs.items()):
    ax.scatter(x, y, s=8, alpha=.6)
    ax.set_title(f"{name}\nPearson r = {np.corrcoef(x, y)[0,1]:.2f}", fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()







Figure 13.1: Strong positive, weak, curved, and none. Only the first is safe for a straight-line model.





Look at the curved one. Its correlation is near zero, and yet x predicts y almost perfectly — just not with a straight line. Correlation only measures straight- line relationships, which is the single most important limitation to remember.


13.1.2 Demo 6 — the real data

import seaborn as sns, matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.6))
ax[0].scatter(homes["area_sqft"], homes["price"]/1e6, s=10, alpha=.5)
ax[0].set_xlabel("Area (sqft)"); ax[0].set_ylabel("₹ millions")
ax[0].set_title("Ignoring city — one cloud")

sns.scatterplot(data=homes, x="area_sqft", y=homes["price"]/1e6,
                hue="city", s=18, alpha=.75, ax=ax[1])
ax[1].set_xlabel("Area (sqft)"); ax[1].set_ylabel("₹ millions")
ax[1].set_title("Coloured by city — three lines")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

for c in ["Mumbai", "Pune", "Nagpur"]:
    sub = homes[homes["city"] == c].dropna()
    r = sub["area_sqft"].corr(sub["price"])
    print(f"{c:<8} {len(sub):>3} houses, area–price correlation {r:.2f}")







Figure 13.2: Area against price, coloured by city. The colour reveals three separate relationships.





Mumbai   193 houses, area–price correlation 0.94
Pune     164 houses, area–price correlation 0.85
Nagpur   118 houses, area–price correlation 0.67


Adding one colour changed the finding. The left chart says “bigger houses cost more, roughly”. The right chart says “bigger houses cost more at a different rate in each city” — which is a far more useful statement, and a modelling instruction.
crumbs: 10  Session 8 — Exploratory Data Analysis and Visualization

title: 10  Session 8 — Exploratory Data Analysis and Visualization
text:
13.2 6. Correlation
Correlation puts a number on how strongly two columns move together. It runs from −1 to +1.



Value
Meaning




+1
perfect: when one rises, the other rises exactly in step


+0.7
strong positive


0
no straight-line relationship


−0.7
strong negative: one rises as the other falls


−1
perfect negative



Two kinds, and they answer different questions:








Kind
Measures
Use when




Pearson
straight-line relationship
the relationship looks linear


Spearman
whether they rise together in rank order
the relationship is curved but consistently increasing




13.2.1 Demo 7 — when Pearson and Spearman disagree

import numpy as np, pandas as pd

cubic = pd.read_csv("datasets/cubic_pair.csv")     # perfectly related, but curved
x, y = cubic["x"], cubic["x_cubed"]

print(f"Pearson  r = {x.corr(y, method='pearson'):.3f}   (straight-line strength)")
print(f"Spearman r = {x.corr(y, method='spearman'):.3f}   (rank agreement)")
print("\nSpearman is exactly 1.0: every time x goes up, y goes up. Always.")
print("Pearson is below 1.0 because the relationship is a curve, not a line.")

Pearson  r = 0.919   (straight-line strength)
Spearman r = 1.000   (rank agreement)

Spearman is exactly 1.0: every time x goes up, y goes up. Always.
Pearson is below 1.0 because the relationship is a curve, not a line.








Tip🧠 Analogy — two dancers



Pearson asks: do they move in step, by the same amount, at the same time?
Spearman asks only: when one steps forward, does the other step forward too? It does not care by how much.
A pair who always move together but with very different stride lengths score perfectly on Spearman and poorly on Pearson.




13.2.2 Demo 8 — the correlation heatmap

import seaborn as sns, matplotlib.pyplot as plt

numeric = homes.select_dtypes("number")
corr = numeric.corr()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 4))
sns.heatmap(corr, annot=True, fmt=".2f", cmap="RdBu_r", center=0,
            vmin=-1, vmax=1, square=True, ax=ax)
ax.set_title("What moves with what?")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print("Correlation with price, strongest first:")
print(corr["price"].drop("price").sort_values(key=abs, ascending=False).round(3))







Figure 13.3: Every numeric pair at once. Read the row for your target column first.





Correlation with price, strongest first:
area_sqft    0.488
bedrooms     0.432
age_years   -0.229
Name: price, dtype: float64


Read the price row first — it ranks your predictors. Then look for very high correlations between predictors: area_sqft and bedrooms are nearly the same column, because bedrooms were derived from area. Keeping both tells a model the same fact twice.






Warning⚠️ Correlation is not causation



Ice cream sales correlate strongly with drowning deaths. Ice cream does not cause drowning: hot weather causes both. A third variable driving two others is called a confounder, and it produces most of the spurious correlations you will meet.
Three things a correlation can mean:

A causes B
B causes A
C causes both — usually this one

A correlation is a question worth investigating, never an answer.




13.2.3 Demo 9 — a confounder, manufactured so you can see it

import numpy as np, pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("datasets/icecream_drownings.csv").rename(
    columns={"temperature_c": "temperature", "ice_cream_sales": "ice_cream"})
print(f"ice cream vs drownings : r = {df['ice_cream'].corr(df['drownings']):.3f}  ← strong!")
print(f"temperature vs ice cream: r = {df['temperature'].corr(df['ice_cream']):.3f}")
print(f"temperature vs drownings: r = {df['temperature'].corr(df['drownings']):.3f}")

# Hold temperature roughly constant and the relationship disappears.
hot_days = df[(df["temperature"] > 30) & (df["temperature"] < 33)]
print(f"\nAmong days between 30-33°C only ({len(hot_days)} days):")
print(f"ice cream vs drownings : r = {hot_days['ice_cream'].corr(hot_days['drownings']):.3f}  ← collapsed")

ice cream vs drownings : r = 0.788  ← strong!
temperature vs ice cream: r = 0.953
temperature vs drownings: r = 0.831

Among days between 30-33°C only (48 days):
ice cream vs drownings : r = 0.233  ← collapsed


The relationship collapsed when temperature was held still — from 0.79 to a value close to zero. That collapse is the signature of a confounder. In the code above we know the truth because we wrote it. With real data you cannot see the arrows — you can only test them.

title: 10  Session 8 — Exploratory Data Analysis and Visualization
text:
14.1 7. Pivot tables
A pivot table summarises one numeric column across two categorical columns — one down the rows, one across the columns. It is the same operation as a groupby, arranged into a grid that a person can read.

14.1.1 Demo 10 — the same data as a groupby and as a pivot

import pandas as pd

print("As a groupby — correct, but hard to scan:")
print(homes.groupby(["city", "bedrooms"])["price"].mean().round(-3).head(8))

print("\nAs a pivot table — the same numbers, laid out to compare:")
pivot = homes.pivot_table(index="city", columns="bedrooms", values="price",
                          aggfunc="mean").round(-3)
print(pivot)

As a groupby — correct, but hard to scan:
city    bedrooms
Mumbai  1            2448000.0
        2            5275000.0
        3            7751000.0
        4           10353000.0
Nagpur  1             538000.0
        2            1101000.0
        3            1639000.0
        4            2577000.0
Name: price, dtype: float64

As a pivot table — the same numbers, laid out to compare:
bedrooms          1          2          3           4
city                                                 
Mumbai    2448000.0  5275000.0  7751000.0  10353000.0
Nagpur     538000.0  1101000.0  1639000.0   2577000.0
Pune       973000.0  2048000.0  3449000.0   4898000.0


Now the comparison is easy in both directions: read across a row to see what an extra bedroom is worth in that city; read down a column to see what the same house costs in different cities.


14.1.2 Demo 11 — pivot tables answer harder questions

print("How many houses in each combination? (check before trusting an average)")
print(homes.pivot_table(index="city", columns="bedrooms", values="price",
                        aggfunc="count", fill_value=0))

print("\nMedian price per square foot, by city and age band:")
homes["age_band"] = pd.cut(homes["age_years"], [0, 10, 20, 40],
                           labels=["new", "middle", "old"], include_lowest=True)
homes["price_per_sqft"] = homes["price"] / homes["area_sqft"]
print(homes.pivot_table(index="city", columns="age_band", values="price_per_sqft",
                        aggfunc="median", observed=True).round(0))

How many houses in each combination? (check before trusting an average)
bedrooms   1   2    3   4
city                     
Mumbai    11  66  110  20
Nagpur     9  37   56  19
Pune      10  65   78  19

Median price per square foot, by city and age band:
age_band     new  middle     old
city                            
Mumbai    6410.0  5971.0  5218.0
Nagpur    1817.0  1207.0   698.0
Pune      3249.0  2703.0  1932.0








Warning⚠️ Always check the counts behind an average



The count table above exists for a reason. An average computed from two houses sits in the grid looking exactly as authoritative as one computed from two hundred. Print the counts next to any pivot of means, or you will act on a cell backed by nothing.




14.1.3 Demo 12 — the pair plot: everything against everything

import seaborn as sns, matplotlib.pyplot as plt

sample = homes[["area_sqft", "age_years", "price", "city"]].dropna().sample(200, random_state=1)
g = sns.pairplot(sample, hue="city", height=1.9, plot_kws={"s": 14, "alpha": .6})
g.figure.suptitle("Everything against everything", y=1.02, fontsize=11)
plt.show()







Figure 14.1: Every numeric column against every other. The diagonal shows each column’s own distribution.





This one chart runs the whole of Part C at once. It is usually the first thing to draw on a new dataset with fewer than about ten numeric columns — and the last thing to draw on one with fifty, where it becomes unreadable.


14.1.4 Demo 13 — the full first pass, as a function

import pandas as pd

def first_look(df, target=None):
    """The five EDA questions, answered in order."""
    print(f"1. SIZE      {df.shape[0]:,} rows × {df.shape[1]} columns")
    num = df.select_dtypes("number").columns.tolist()
    cat = df.select_dtypes(exclude="number").columns.tolist()
    print(f"   numeric   {num}")
    print(f"   other     {cat}")

    miss = df.isna().sum()
    miss = miss[miss > 0]
    print(f"\n2. MISSING   {'none' if miss.empty else miss.to_dict()}")

    print("\n3. SHAPE OF EACH NUMERIC COLUMN")
    for c in num:
        s = df[c].dropna()
        lean = "right" if s.skew() > .5 else "left" if s.skew() < -.5 else "symmetric"
        print(f"   {c:<16} median {s.median():>12,.0f}   skew {s.skew():>6.2f} ({lean})")

    print("\n4. CATEGORY COUNTS")
    for c in cat:
        print(f"   {c:<16} {df[c].value_counts().to_dict()}")

    if target:
        print(f"\n5. WHAT MOVES WITH {target.upper()}")
        print(df[num].corr()[target].drop(target).sort_values(key=abs, ascending=False).round(3).to_string())

first_look(homes[["area_sqft", "age_years", "bedrooms", "price", "city"]], target="price")

1. SIZE      500 rows × 5 columns
   numeric   ['area_sqft', 'age_years', 'bedrooms', 'price']
   other     ['city']

2. MISSING   {'area_sqft': 25}

3. SHAPE OF EACH NUMERIC COLUMN
   area_sqft        median        1,209   skew  -0.18 (symmetric)
   age_years        median           19   skew   0.07 (symmetric)
   bedrooms         median            3   skew  -0.17 (symmetric)
   price            median    3,582,500   skew   0.59 (right)

4. CATEGORY COUNTS
   city             {'Mumbai': 207, 'Pune': 172, 'Nagpur': 121}

5. WHAT MOVES WITH PRICE
area_sqft    0.488
bedrooms     0.432
age_years   -0.229




14.1.5 ❓ Check yourself
Q1. You want to know whether house prices differ between three cities. Which chart?


A scatter plot.


A box plot of price grouped by city.


A pie chart of cities.


Q2. Two columns have a Pearson correlation of 0.02, but the scatter plot shows a clear U shape. What does that mean?


The correlation was computed wrongly.


They are strongly related, but not in a straight line — Pearson cannot see it.


They are unrelated.


Q3. area_sqft and bedrooms correlate at 0.93. What should you do?


Nothing; strong correlations are good.


Note that they carry nearly the same information, and consider keeping only one.


Delete both.


Q4. A pivot table cell shows an average price of ₹4.2 crore. What must you check before quoting it?


That the currency is correct.


How many rows that average is computed from.


Whether the column is numeric.








NoteAnswers





A1 — (b). One numeric column split by one categorical column — the box-plot-by-group row of the chart chooser.
A2 — (b). Demo 5’s third panel: near-zero correlation, near-perfect relationship.
A3 — (b). In this dataset bedrooms were derived from area, so they genuinely are one fact. Session 6’s feature selection is the tool.
A4 — (b). Demo 11’s warning. An average of two houses looks identical to an average of two hundred.

text:
11.1 🎯 Learning outcomes
By the end of this chapter you can:

title: 11  Session 9 — Supervised Learning Techniques
text:
Explain supervised learning and why it needs labelled data.
Tell a regression problem from a classification problem.
Fit a simple linear regression and read its slope and intercept as a sentence.
Fit a multiple regression and interpret a coefficient correctly.
Report MAE, RMSE and R², and say which to quote to whom.
Compare a model against a baseline and say whether it earned its place.
Name three assumptions linear regression makes and check one.

title: 11  Session 9 — Supervised Learning Techniques
text:
11.2 How this chapter is organised



Part
Question it answers




A — What supervised learning is
How does a machine learn from examples?


B — Simple regression
How do I predict a number from one input?


C — Multiple regression
And from several inputs?


D — Measuring it
Is the prediction any good?

title: 11  Session 9 — Supervised Learning Techniques
text:
12.1 1. Learning from labelled examples
Supervised learning trains an algorithm on historical data where the answer is already known. The known answer is called the label or the target.
You do not tell the algorithm the rule. You show it thousands of examples with their answers, and it works the rule out.






Tip🧠 Analogy — flashcards



A student revising with flashcards:

the front of the card is the input — the features
the back is the answer — the label
learning is guessing, flipping the card, and adjusting

Where it breaks down: a student understands why the answer is what it is. A model only finds a pattern that fits. Show it enough cards where the answer happens to correlate with the card’s colour, and it will learn colour.


The two vocabulary words used everywhere from here on:



Word
Means
Written as




Features
the inputs you know
X — a table, capital X


Target
the answer you want
y — one column, lowercase y

title: 11  Session 9 — Supervised Learning Techniques
text:
12.2 2. Regression or classification?
Every supervised problem is one of two kinds, decided entirely by what the target looks like.










Target is
Question
Examples




Regression
a number
how much? how many?
house price, tomorrow’s temperature, delivery time


Classification
a category
which one? yes or no?
spam or not, will they default, which disease



This chapter is regression. Session 10’s clustering and later work covers the rest.

12.2.1 Demo 1 — telling them apart

problems = [
    ("Predict a flat's monthly rent",                 "₹28,400",        "number"),
    ("Will this customer cancel their subscription?", "yes / no",       "category"),
    ("How many units will we sell next month?",       "1,840",          "number"),
    ("Which of 5 categories is this news article?",   "sport",          "category"),
    ("What score out of 10 will this film get?",      "7.3",            "number"),
]
print(f"{'problem':<48} {'answer looks like':<18} {'task'}")
print("-" * 84)
for q, example, kind in problems:
    print(f"{q:<48} {example:<18} {'REGRESSION' if kind=='number' else 'CLASSIFICATION'}")

problem                                          answer looks like  task
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Predict a flat's monthly rent                    ₹28,400            REGRESSION
Will this customer cancel their subscription?    yes / no           CLASSIFICATION
How many units will we sell next month?          1,840              REGRESSION
Which of 5 categories is this news article?      sport              CLASSIFICATION
What score out of 10 will this film get?         7.3                REGRESSION








Warning⚠️ A number is not always a regression target



A rating of 1 to 5 looks numeric. But if the gap between 1 and 2 does not mean the same as the gap between 4 and 5, treating it as a number is a claim about the world you may not want to make. Ask what the number measures, not what type it is stored as.

title: 11  Session 9 — Supervised Learning Techniques
text:
13.1 3. One input, one line
Simple linear regression draws the single straight line that comes closest to all your data points, and uses it to predict.
The line is described by two numbers:
\[\text{prediction} = \text{intercept} + \text{slope} \times \text{input}\]







Number
Means




slope
how much the prediction changes for a one-unit increase in the input


intercept
the prediction when the input is zero



“Closest” has a precise meaning: the line that makes the sum of the squared vertical distances to the points as small as possible. Squared, for the same reason as in Session 7 — so that errors above and below the line cannot cancel out.

13.1.1 Demo 2 — fitting one line, and reading it out loud

import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

import pandas as pd

emp = pd.read_csv("datasets/experience_salary.csv")
experience, salary = emp["experience_years"].values, emp["salary"].values
print(emp.head(3), f"\n\n{len(emp)} employees on file\n")

X = experience.reshape(-1, 1)          # scikit-learn wants a 2-D table, even for one column
y = salary

model = LinearRegression().fit(X, y)
line = model.predict(X)

plt.scatter(experience, salary, s=25, label="actual people")
order = np.argsort(experience)
plt.plot(experience[order], line[order], "r-", lw=2, label="the fitted line")
for xi, yi, pi in zip(experience, salary, line):
    plt.plot([xi, xi], [yi, pi], color="grey", lw=.6, alpha=.6)
plt.xlabel("Years of experience"); plt.ylabel("Salary (₹)"); plt.legend()
plt.show()

print(f"intercept = ₹{model.intercept_:,.0f}")
print(f"slope     = ₹{model.coef_[0]:,.0f} per year of experience")
print(f"\nRead as a sentence:")
print(f'  "Someone with no experience earns about ₹{model.intercept_:,.0f}.')
print(f'   Each additional year is worth about ₹{model.coef_[0]:,.0f}."')

   experience_years    salary
0             13.55  121356.0
1              1.02   31755.0
2             10.09  123457.0 

40 employees on file









Figure 13.1: The line of best fit. Grey lines are the residuals — the errors the fit is minimising.





intercept = ₹18,241
slope     = ₹9,725 per year of experience

Read as a sentence:
  "Someone with no experience earns about ₹18,241.
   Each additional year is worth about ₹9,725."




13.1.2 Demo 3 — using it to predict

import pandas as pd

for years in [0, 3, 7, 12]:
    pred = model.predict([[years]])[0]
    print(f"{years:>2} years of experience → predicted salary ₹{pred:>9,.0f}")

print(f"\n40 years of experience → ₹{model.predict([[40]])[0]:,.0f}")
print("  ⚠ nobody in the training data had more than 15 years. This number is a")
print("    guess about territory the model has never seen — it is extrapolation.")

 0 years of experience → predicted salary ₹   18,241
 3 years of experience → predicted salary ₹   47,417
 7 years of experience → predicted salary ₹   86,318
12 years of experience → predicted salary ₹  134,944

40 years of experience → ₹407,253
  ⚠ nobody in the training data had more than 15 years. This number is a
    guess about territory the model has never seen — it is extrapolation.








Warning⚠️ The intercept is often meaningless



Here “zero years of experience” is a real situation, so the intercept means something. But in a model predicting house price from area, the intercept is the price of a house with zero square feet — a number the maths needs and the world does not have.
Do not report an intercept as a finding unless zero is a real value for that input.

title: 11  Session 9 — Supervised Learning Techniques
text:
14.1 4. Several inputs at once
Multiple regression uses two or more features. Instead of a line through a scatter plot, it fits a flat surface through a cloud — but the code is identical, and so is the interpretation, with one crucial addition.
\[\text{price} = \text{intercept} + b_1 \times \text{area} + b_2 \times \text{bedrooms} + b_3 \times \text{age}\]






Important🔓 What a coefficient means, exactly



A coefficient is the effect of that feature while every other feature is held constant.
That phrase is the whole thing. “Each extra bedroom adds ₹4 lakh” is wrong. “Each extra bedroom adds ₹4 lakh, comparing houses of the same area and age” is right — and it is a completely different claim, because bigger houses usually have more bedrooms anyway.



14.1.1 Demo 4 — a real multiple regression, done properly

import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error, r2_score

homes = pd.read_csv("datasets/house_prices.csv")
print(f"{len(homes)} houses on file: {list(homes.columns)}\n")

# The file was built from a known truth, so we can check what the model recovers:
#   ₹3,200 per square foot · ₹250,000 per bedroom · −₹45,000 per year of age

X = homes[["area_sqft", "bedrooms", "age_years"]]
y = homes["price"]
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=0)

model = LinearRegression().fit(X_train, y_train)

print("What the model learned:")
for name, coef in zip(X.columns, model.coef_):
    print(f"  {name:<12} {coef:>12,.0f}")
print(f"  {'intercept':<12} {model.intercept_:>12,.0f}")

print("\nRead as sentences (each holds the others constant):")
print(f"  one more square foot  → ₹{model.coef_[0]:>10,.0f}   (same bedrooms, same age)")
print(f"  one more bedroom      → ₹{model.coef_[1]:>10,.0f}   (same area, same age)")
print(f"  one more year of age  → ₹{model.coef_[2]:>10,.0f}   (same area, same bedrooms)")

400 houses on file: ['area_sqft', 'bedrooms', 'age_years', 'price']

What the model learned:
  area_sqft           3,051
  bedrooms          291,399
  age_years         -44,476
  intercept         436,494

Read as sentences (each holds the others constant):
  one more square foot  → ₹     3,051   (same bedrooms, same age)
  one more bedroom      → ₹   291,399   (same area, same age)
  one more year of age  → ₹   -44,476   (same area, same bedrooms)




14.1.2 Demo 5 — why “holding constant” changes the answer

from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

alone = LinearRegression().fit(X_train[["bedrooms"]], y_train)
print(f"bedrooms ALONE          : ₹{alone.coef_[0]:>12,.0f} per bedroom")
print(f"bedrooms WITH area, age : ₹{model.coef_[1]:>12,.0f} per bedroom")
print(f"\ncorrelation between area and bedrooms: {X_train['area_sqft'].corr(X_train['bedrooms']):.2f}")

bedrooms ALONE          : ₹   1,492,208 per bedroom
bedrooms WITH area, age : ₹     291,399 per bedroom

correlation between area and bedrooms: 0.95


On its own, a bedroom looks worth far more. That is because bedrooms come attached to floor area, and the single-feature model credits the bedroom with the area’s effect too. Once area is in the model, the bedroom coefficient reports only what a bedroom adds by itself.






Warning⚠️ Highly correlated features make coefficients unreliable



When two features carry nearly the same information — as area and bedrooms do here — the model can split the credit between them almost arbitrarily. The predictions stay fine; the individual coefficients become unstable and should not be quoted as findings. This is called multicollinearity, and Session 8’s heatmap is how you spot it coming.




14.1.3 Demo 6 — adding features one at a time

import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score, mean_absolute_error

sets = [["area_sqft"],
        ["area_sqft", "bedrooms"],
        ["area_sqft", "bedrooms", "age_years"]]

print(f"{'features':<40} {'test R²':>9} {'test MAE':>14}")
print("-" * 65)
for cols in sets:
    m = LinearRegression().fit(X_train[cols], y_train)
    pred = m.predict(X_test[cols])
    print(f"{', '.join(cols):<40} {r2_score(y_test, pred):>9.3f} {mean_absolute_error(y_test, pred):>14,.0f}")

features                                   test R²       test MAE
-----------------------------------------------------------------
area_sqft                                    0.868        473,788
area_sqft, bedrooms                          0.866        484,325
area_sqft, bedrooms, age_years               0.971        206,858


Adding bedrooms made the model very slightly worse — 0.868 down to 0.866. Area already carried that information, so the extra column brought no signal and a little noise. Adding age_years improved R² from 0.87 to 0.97 and more than halved the typical error, because age is genuinely new information that area cannot supply.
That is the whole of feature selection in one table: a column earns its place by improving the score on data the model has not seen, not by sounding relevant. Session 6 automates exactly this comparison.

title: 11  Session 9 — Supervised Learning Techniques
text:
15.1 5. The three regression metrics
A prediction is never exactly right. The metric decides how you count the misses.









Metric
What it is
Units
Character




MAE
average size of the error
same as the target
treats all errors evenly


RMSE
square root of the average squared error
same as the target
punishes large errors much harder


R²
share of the variation the model explains
none — a fraction
1.0 perfect, 0 no better than the average




15.1.1 Demo 7 — computed by hand, then by scikit-learn

import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error, r2_score

import pandas as pd

preds = pd.read_csv("datasets/predictions_small.csv")
actual, predicted = preds["actual"].values, preds["predicted"].values
errors = predicted - actual

print(f"actual    : {actual.tolist()}")
print(f"predicted : {predicted.tolist()}")
print(f"errors    : {errors.tolist()}")

print(f"\nMAE  = average of |errors|      = {np.abs(errors).mean():.2f}")
print(f"RMSE = √(average of errors²)    = {np.sqrt((errors**2).mean()):.2f}")

ss_res = (errors ** 2).sum()
ss_tot = ((actual - actual.mean()) ** 2).sum()
print(f"R²   = 1 - {ss_res} / {ss_tot:.0f} = {1 - ss_res/ss_tot:.4f}")

print(f"\nscikit-learn agrees: MAE {mean_absolute_error(actual, predicted):.2f}, "
      f"RMSE {np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(actual, predicted)):.2f}, "
      f"R² {r2_score(actual, predicted):.4f}")

actual    : [100, 200, 300, 400, 500]
predicted : [110, 190, 310, 380, 520]
errors    : [10, -10, 10, -20, 20]

MAE  = average of |errors|      = 14.00
RMSE = √(average of errors²)    = 14.83
R²   = 1 - 1100 / 100000 = 0.9890

scikit-learn agrees: MAE 14.00, RMSE 14.83, R² 0.9890




15.1.2 Demo 8 — why MAE and RMSE disagree, and when it matters

import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error

import pandas as pd

pat = pd.read_csv("datasets/two_error_patterns.csv")
actual = pat["actual"].values

for name, pred in [("everything off by 20", pat["model_a_spread_out"].values),
                   ("99 perfect, 1 wrong by 2000", pat["model_b_one_disaster"].values)]:
    mae = mean_absolute_error(actual, pred)
    rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(actual, pred))
    print(f"{name:<30} MAE {mae:7.2f}   RMSE {rmse:7.2f}")

everything off by 20           MAE   20.00   RMSE   20.00
99 perfect, 1 wrong by 2000    MAE   20.00   RMSE  200.00


Both models have the same MAE. RMSE separates them completely, because it squares the errors before averaging — so one enormous mistake counts for far more than a hundred small ones.
Which to report:








If
Use
Because




all errors cost the same
MAE
it is the plain average error, and it is easy to explain


one big error is disastrous — a bridge, a dosage, a delivery promise
RMSE
it makes large errors visible


you are talking to a non-technical audience
MAE
“we are typically off by ₹2 lakh” needs no explanation


you are comparing across different datasets
R²
it has no units





15.1.3 Demo 9 — always compare against a baseline

import numpy as np
from sklearn.dummy import DummyRegressor
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, r2_score

baseline = DummyRegressor(strategy="mean").fit(X_train, y_train)   # always predicts the average
real     = LinearRegression().fit(X_train, y_train)

for name, m in [("Baseline (always the mean)", baseline), ("Linear regression", real)]:
    pred = m.predict(X_test)
    print(f"{name:<28} MAE ₹{mean_absolute_error(y_test, pred):>10,.0f}   R² {r2_score(y_test, pred):>7.3f}")

improvement = 1 - mean_absolute_error(y_test, real.predict(X_test)) / \
                  mean_absolute_error(y_test, baseline.predict(X_test))
print(f"\nThe model reduced the typical error by {improvement:.0%} versus guessing the average.")

Baseline (always the mean)   MAE ₹ 1,222,939   R²  -0.011
Linear regression            MAE ₹   206,858   R²   0.971

The model reduced the typical error by 83% versus guessing the average.








Important🔓 R² of 0 means ‘no better than the average’



That is exactly what the baseline scores. R² is defined against that baseline, so a model with R² of 0.02 has essentially learned nothing, and a negative R² means it is worse than always guessing the mean.
Always run the baseline. It converts “R² is 0.62” — which sounds like a number someone could argue about — into “the model cuts the typical error by a third”, which is a business fact.

title: 11  Session 9 — Supervised Learning Techniques
text:
15.2 6. Checking the assumptions
Linear regression assumes things about your data. When they are false, the predictions can still work — but the coefficients and confidence in them cannot be trusted.








Assumption
Means
How to check




Linearity
the relationship really is a straight line
residual plot


Constant spread
errors are equally large everywhere
residual plot


Independence
one row’s error tells you nothing about the next
know how the data was collected


No severe multicollinearity
features are not near-copies of each other
correlation heatmap




15.2.1 Demo 10 — the residual plot, and the two shapes that condemn a model

import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

import pandas as pd

rs = pd.read_csv("datasets/residual_shapes.csv")
x = rs["x"].values
cases = {
    "Healthy":        rs["healthy"].values,
    "Curved pattern": rs["curved"].values,
    "Fanning out":    rs["fanning_out"].values,
}

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.2))
for ax, (name, yy) in zip(axes, cases.items()):
    m = LinearRegression().fit(x.reshape(-1, 1), yy)
    resid = yy - m.predict(x.reshape(-1, 1))
    ax.scatter(m.predict(x.reshape(-1, 1)), resid, s=10, alpha=.6)
    ax.axhline(0, color="red", lw=1.5)
    ax.set_title(name, fontsize=10); ax.set_xlabel("predicted"); ax.set_ylabel("error")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print("A residual plot should look like a shapeless cloud centred on zero.")
print("  A CURVE  → the true relationship is not a straight line; add a squared term")
print("             or use a model that can bend.")
print("  A FAN    → errors grow with the size of the prediction. The model is far less")
print("             reliable for large values than the single R² suggests.")







Figure 15.1: Left: a healthy residual plot — formless cloud around zero. Middle: a curve, so the relationship is not linear. Right: a fan, so error grows with size.





A residual plot should look like a shapeless cloud centred on zero.
  A CURVE  → the true relationship is not a straight line; add a squared term
             or use a model that can bend.
  A FAN    → errors grow with the size of the prediction. The model is far less
             reliable for large values than the single R² suggests.


Session 11 goes further with this. For now: draw the residual plot before you believe the R².


15.2.2 Demo 11 — when the straight line is the wrong shape

import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score

fuel = pd.read_csv("datasets/fuel_efficiency.csv")
speed, efficiency = fuel["speed_kmh"].values, fuel["efficiency_kmpl"].values
# Efficiency peaks in the middle and falls at both ends — a curve, not a line.

Xs = speed.reshape(-1, 1)
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(Xs, efficiency, test_size=.3, random_state=0)

straight = LinearRegression().fit(Xtr, ytr)
curved   = make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(2), LinearRegression()).fit(Xtr, ytr)

print(f"straight line       R² = {r2_score(yte, straight.predict(Xte)):.3f}")
print(f"curve (degree 2)    R² = {r2_score(yte, curved.predict(Xte)):.3f}")
print("\nThe straight line explains almost nothing, because efficiency rises then falls.")
print("`PolynomialFeatures(2)` adds a squared term, and the same LinearRegression")
print("then fits a curve — the model is still 'linear' in its coefficients.")

straight line       R² = 0.173
curve (degree 2)    R² = 0.940

The straight line explains almost nothing, because efficiency rises then falls.
`PolynomialFeatures(2)` adds a squared term, and the same LinearRegression
then fits a curve — the model is still 'linear' in its coefficients.




15.2.3 ❓ Check yourself
Q1. A bank predicts whether a customer will default (yes/no). What kind of task?


Regression.


Classification.


Neither.


Q2. In a multiple regression the coefficient on bedrooms is ₹250,000. What does it mean?


Every house with a bedroom is worth ₹250,000 more.


Comparing houses of the same area and age, an extra bedroom adds about ₹250,000.


Bedrooms cost ₹250,000 to build.


Q3. Model A: every prediction off by 20. Model B: 99 perfect, one off by 2,000. Which metric separates them?


MAE.


RMSE.


Neither.


Q4. Your model scores R² = 0.02 on the test set. What does that mean?


It is 2% accurate.


It is barely better than always predicting the average.


It is 98% wrong.


Q5. A residual plot fans out as predictions grow. What does that tell you?


The model is broken.


Errors grow with the size of the prediction, so the model is less reliable for large values than the overall score suggests.


There is a missing feature.








NoteAnswers





A1 — (b). The target is a category.
A2 — (b). The “holding everything else constant” clause is the whole meaning of a coefficient. Demo 5 showed the number more than doubling without it.
A3 — (b). Demo 8 measured identical MAEs and very different RMSEs.
A4 — (b). R² is defined against the always-predict-the-mean baseline, so 0.02 means almost no improvement on it.
A5 — (b). Demo 10’s third panel. Quote the R² alone and you overstate reliability for exactly the expensive cases.

title: 12  Session 10 — Unsupervised Learning and Clustering
text:
13.1 1. Unsupervised learning
Unsupervised learning finds structure in data that has no target column. Nobody has labelled anything; the algorithm has only the features.









Supervised (Session 9)
Unsupervised (this chapter)




Data
X and y
X only


Goal
predict y for new rows
find structure in X


Can you measure accuracy?
yes — compare to the true y
no — there is no true answer


Fails by
predicting badly
producing groups that mean nothing



Three families:








Family
Finds
Covered in




Clustering
groups of similar rows
this chapter


Dimensionality reduction
a smaller set of columns
Session 6 (PCA)


Association rules
things that occur together
Session 16









Tip🧠 Analogy — sorting the laundry



Nobody told you the categories. You tip the basket out and start making piles — darks, whites, towels — because things in a pile resemble each other.
Somebody else would make different piles. By fabric, perhaps, or by owner. Neither is wrong. That is unsupervised learning: several defensible answers, and no marking scheme.

title: 12  Session 10 — Unsupervised Learning and Clustering
text:
13.2 2. What clustering is for
Clustering puts rows into groups so that rows in a group are more similar to each other than to rows in other groups.



Use
What the clusters become




Customer segmentation
marketing groups with different offers


Document grouping
topics


Image compression
a small palette of representative colours


Anomaly detection
whatever does not fit any cluster


Exploration
the first look at data nobody has labelled



“Similar” means “close together” — so clustering is a distance calculation, and every warning from Session 5 about scale applies with full force.

title: 12  Session 10 — Unsupervised Learning and Clustering
text:
14.1 3. How K-Means works
K-Means splits data into k groups by repeatedly moving k centre points until they settle.





flowchart TB
    S1["<b>1.</b> Pick k. Place k centres at random"]
    S2["<b>2.</b> Assign every point to its<br/>nearest centre"]
    S3["<b>3.</b> Move each centre to the average<br/>of the points assigned to it"]
    S4{"Did anything<br/>move?"}
    S1 --> S2 --> S3 --> S4
    S4 -- yes --> S2
    S4 -- no --> S5["<b>Done.</b> The centres have settled"]






You must choose k yourself. The algorithm cannot tell you how many groups exist — that is the whole difficulty, and Part C is about it.

14.1.1 Demo 1 — watching the centres settle, step by step

import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt

import pandas as pd

points = pd.read_csv("datasets/three_blobs.csv")[["x", "y"]].values

centres = np.array([[1., 6.], [2., 7.], [3., 6.5]])   # deliberately bad starting positions

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(13, 3.1))
for step, ax in enumerate(axes):
    distances = np.linalg.norm(points[:, None] - centres[None], axis=2)
    labels = distances.argmin(axis=1)                       # step 2: assign
    ax.scatter(points[:, 0], points[:, 1], c=labels, s=12, cmap="viridis")
    ax.scatter(centres[:, 0], centres[:, 1], c="red", marker="X", s=150, edgecolor="k")
    ax.set_title(f"iteration {step}", fontsize=10); ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
    for j in range(3):                                       # step 3: move
        if (labels == j).any():
            centres[j] = points[labels == j].mean(axis=0)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print("Started at:", [[1., 6.], [2., 7.], [3., 6.5]], "— all three bunched in one corner")
print("Ended at:  ", centres.round(1).tolist())
print("The true centres were [2,2], [7,3], [4,7].")







Figure 14.1: Four iterations of K-Means. The crosses are the centres; watch them walk into place.





Started at: [[1.0, 6.0], [2.0, 7.0], [3.0, 6.5]] — all three bunched in one corner
Ended at:   [[1.9, 2.0], [4.1, 7.0], [7.0, 3.0]]
The true centres were [2,2], [7,3], [4,7].




14.1.2 Demo 2 — the same thing with scikit-learn

import numpy as np, pandas as pd, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

# A real dataset: 200 mall customers, their annual income and a spending score
# the mall assigned them.
customers = pd.read_csv("datasets/Mall_Customers.csv").rename(columns={
    "Annual Income (k$)": "income", "Spending Score (1-100)": "spending_score"})
print(customers.head(3), f"\n\n{len(customers)} customers on file\n")

km = KMeans(n_clusters=5, random_state=0, n_init=10)
customers["cluster"] = km.fit_predict(customers[["income", "spending_score"]])

plt.scatter(customers["income"], customers["spending_score"],
            c=customers["cluster"], cmap="viridis", s=18)
plt.scatter(km.cluster_centers_[:, 0], km.cluster_centers_[:, 1],
            c="red", marker="X", s=220, edgecolor="k", label="centres")
plt.xlabel("Annual income (k$)"); plt.ylabel("Spending score"); plt.legend()
plt.show()

print(customers.groupby("cluster").agg(
    n=("income", "size"), avg_income=("income", "mean"), avg_spend=("spending_score", "mean")
).round(1))

   CustomerID  Gender  Age  income  spending_score
0           1    Male   19      15              39
1           2    Male   21      15              81
2           3  Female   20      16               6 

200 customers on file









Figure 14.2: Customer segments by income and spending score, with the centres marked.





          n  avg_income  avg_spend
cluster                           
0        81        55.3       49.5
1        39        86.5       82.1
2        35        88.2       17.1
3        23        26.3       20.9
4        22        25.7       79.4


Note n_init=10: K-Means starts from random positions and can settle into a poor arrangement, so it runs ten times from different starts and keeps the best.

title: 12  Session 10 — Unsupervised Learning and Clustering
text:
14.2 4. Scale first — always
K-Means measures straight-line distance. An unscaled column with big numbers decides every cluster on its own.
This is Session 5’s lesson, and clustering is where it does the most damage — because there is no accuracy score to warn you that the answer is wrong.

14.2.1 Demo 3 — real data where the scales genuinely differ
The mall file happens to be convenient: income in thousands (range 122) and spending score out of 100 (range 98) are already on comparable scales, so scaling would change almost nothing. Check before you assume you need it.

import pandas as pd

mall = pd.read_csv("datasets/Mall_Customers.csv").rename(columns={
    "Annual Income (k$)": "income", "Spending Score (1-100)": "spending_score"})
print("Mall file — the two columns are already comparable:")
for c in ["income", "spending_score"]:
    print(f"  {c:<15} range {mall[c].max() - mall[c].min():>10,.0f}")

Mall file — the two columns are already comparable:
  income          range        122
  spending_score  range         98


Now a real file where they are not. loan_data_10k.csv records income in rupees (hundreds of thousands) next to loan-to-income ratio (a fraction between 0 and 1).

import pandas as pd, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

loan = (pd.read_csv("datasets/loan_data_10k.csv")
          .dropna(subset=["person_income", "loan_percent_income"])
          .sample(2_000, random_state=0))
X = loan[["person_income", "loan_percent_income"]]

print("Loan file — the two columns are not remotely comparable:")
for c in X.columns:
    print(f"  {c:<22} range {X[c].max() - X[c].min():>13,.2f}")

unscaled_labels = KMeans(4, random_state=0, n_init=10).fit_predict(X)
scaled_labels = KMeans(4, random_state=0, n_init=10).fit_predict(StandardScaler().fit_transform(X))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.6))
ax[0].scatter(X["person_income"], X["loan_percent_income"], c=unscaled_labels,
              cmap="viridis", s=6, alpha=.6)
ax[0].set_title("Unscaled — boundaries are vertical")
ax[1].scatter(X["person_income"], X["loan_percent_income"], c=scaled_labels,
              cmap="viridis", s=6, alpha=.6)
ax[1].set_title("Scaled — both columns count")
for a in ax:
    a.set_xlabel("Income (₹)"); a.set_ylabel("Loan as a share of income"); a.set_xscale("log")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

agree = pd.crosstab(unscaled_labels, scaled_labels).max(axis=1).sum() / len(X)
print(f"\nUnscaled, an income gap of ₹1,000 outweighs the entire 0-to-1 ratio scale.")
print(f"The two clusterings agree on only {agree:.0%} of applicants —")
print(f"{1 - agree:.0%} land in a completely different group depending on whether you scaled.")

Loan file — the two columns are not remotely comparable:
  person_income          range    832,912.00
  loan_percent_income    range          0.53








Figure 14.3: Left: unscaled, so income alone decides and the boundaries are vertical. Right: scaled, so both columns count.






Unscaled, an income gap of ₹1,000 outweighs the entire 0-to-1 ratio scale.
The two clusterings agree on only 57% of applicants —
43% land in a completely different group depending on whether you scaled.








Warning⚠️ Unscaled clustering produces confident nonsense



No error is raised. The clusters look tidy, the chart is colourful, and 43% of applicants are in a different group purely because of a unit choice.
Put StandardScaler in front of KMeans unless you have checked that the columns are already comparable — and check by printing the ranges, as the first cell above does.

title: 12  Session 10 — Unsupervised Learning and Clustering
text:
15.1 5. The elbow method
Inertia is the total squared distance from every point to its own centre. More clusters always means lower inertia — with one cluster per point it reaches zero — so you cannot simply minimise it.
The elbow method looks for the point where the improvement stops being worth it.

15.1.1 Demo 4 — the elbow

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

Xs = StandardScaler().fit_transform(customers[["income", "spending_score"]])

ks = range(1, 9)
inertias = [KMeans(k, random_state=0, n_init=10).fit(Xs).inertia_ for k in ks]

plt.plot(ks, inertias, "o-")
plt.axvline(5, color="red", ls="--", alpha=.6)
plt.xlabel("k (number of clusters)"); plt.ylabel("inertia")
plt.title("Where does the line stop dropping steeply?")
plt.show()

print(f"{'k':>3} {'inertia':>10} {'improvement':>13}")
for i, (k, v) in enumerate(zip(ks, inertias)):
    imp = "" if i == 0 else f"{(inertias[i-1]-v)/inertias[i-1]:>12.1%}"
    print(f"{k:>3} {v:>10.1f} {imp:>13}")







Figure 15.1: Inertia falls with every extra cluster. The bend at k=5 is where extra clusters stop paying.





  k    inertia   improvement
  1      400.0              
  2      269.3         32.7%
  3      157.7         41.4%
  4      108.9         30.9%
  5       65.6         39.8%
  6       55.1         15.9%
  7       44.9         18.5%
  8       37.1         17.3%


Read the improvement column: large gains up to k=5, then much smaller ones. That is the elbow — and five is the answer this well-known dataset is famous for.
crumbs: 12  Session 10 — Unsupervised Learning and Clustering

title: 12  Session 10 — Unsupervised Learning and Clustering
text:
15.2 6. The silhouette score
The silhouette score measures, for each point, how much closer it is to its own cluster than to the next nearest one. It runs from −1 to +1.







Score
Means




near +1
comfortably inside its own cluster


near 0
on the boundary — could belong to either


negative
closer to a different cluster — probably misassigned



Unlike inertia, it does not automatically improve with more clusters, so you can compare values across different k directly.

15.2.1 Demo 5 — silhouette across k

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score

ks = range(2, 9)
scores = [silhouette_score(Xs, KMeans(k, random_state=0, n_init=10).fit_predict(Xs)) for k in ks]

plt.plot(list(ks), scores, "o-", color="darkgreen")
best = list(ks)[int(np.argmax(scores))]
plt.axvline(best, color="red", ls="--", alpha=.6)
plt.xlabel("k"); plt.ylabel("silhouette score"); plt.title("Higher is better")
plt.show()

for k, s in zip(ks, scores):
    print(f"k = {k}: silhouette {s:.3f}{'   ← best' if k == best else ''}")







Figure 15.2: Silhouette by k. Unlike inertia, higher is genuinely better, so the peak is the answer.





k = 2: silhouette 0.286
k = 3: silhouette 0.467
k = 4: silhouette 0.494
k = 5: silhouette 0.555   ← best
k = 6: silhouette 0.538
k = 7: silhouette 0.526
k = 8: silhouette 0.457


Both methods point at the same answer here. They do not always.


15.2.2 Demo 6 — when the silhouette score is wrong

import numpy as np
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score

# Two interleaved crescents. The true structure is obviously 2 groups.
mo = pd.read_csv("datasets/moons.csv")
moons = mo[["x", "y"]].values
true_labels = mo["true_group"].values

for k in [2, 3, 4]:
    labels = KMeans(k, random_state=0, n_init=10).fit_predict(moons)
    print(f"k = {k}: silhouette {silhouette_score(moons, labels):.3f}")

agree = (KMeans(2, random_state=0, n_init=10).fit_predict(moons) == true_labels)
print(f"\nAt k=2, K-Means agrees with the true crescents for "
      f"{max(agree.mean(), 1-agree.mean()):.0%} of points.")
print("The score prefers k=2, and yet K-Means still cuts the crescents in the wrong")
print("place — because it can only draw straight boundaries. A good score does not")
print("mean a good clustering.")

k = 2: silhouette 0.489
k = 3: silhouette 0.428
k = 4: silhouette 0.461

At k=2, K-Means agrees with the true crescents for 76% of points.
The score prefers k=2, and yet K-Means still cuts the crescents in the wrong
place — because it can only draw straight boundaries. A good score does not
mean a good clustering.








Warning⚠️ Clustering always returns clusters



Ask K-Means for four groups in pure random noise and you will get four groups, each with a centre and a colour, and a chart that looks meaningful.

import numpy as np
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score

noise = pd.read_csv("datasets/random_noise.csv")[["x", "y"]].values   # no structure at all
for k in [2, 3, 4]:
    print(f"k = {k} on pure noise: silhouette {silhouette_score(noise, KMeans(k, random_state=0, n_init=10).fit_predict(noise)):.3f}")

k = 2 on pure noise: silhouette 0.314
k = 3 on pure noise: silhouette 0.326
k = 4 on pure noise: silhouette 0.321


Those are not zero. The elbow and the silhouette are evidence, not proof. The real test is whether the clusters mean something to somebody who knows the business.

title: 12  Session 10 — Unsupervised Learning and Clustering
section: 15.3 7. Profiling: turning clusters into an answer
text:
15.3 7. Profiling: turning clusters into an answer
A cluster number is not a deliverable. cluster = 2 means nothing to a marketing team. The deliverable is a description.

15.3.1 Demo 7 — from cluster numbers to named segments

import pandas as pd
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

X = customers[["income", "spending_score"]]
customers["segment"] = KMeans(5, random_state=0, n_init=10).fit_predict(
    StandardScaler().fit_transform(X))

profile = customers.groupby("segment").agg(
    customers=("income", "size"),
    median_income=("income", "median"),
    median_spend=("spending_score", "median"),
).round(0)
profile["share"] = (profile["customers"] / len(customers) * 100).round(1).astype(str) + "%"
print(profile)

print("\nNow name them, and say what to do:")
overall_income = customers["income"].median()
overall_spend = customers["spending_score"].median()
for seg, row in profile.iterrows():
    rich = "high" if row["median_income"] > overall_income else "modest"
    spends = "high" if row["median_spend"] > overall_spend else "low"
    name = {("high", "high"): "Best customers — reward and retain",
            ("high", "low"):  "Untapped — money, but not spending here",
            ("modest", "low"): "Budget-conscious — low priority",
            ("modest", "high"): "Enthusiasts on a budget — grow carefully"}[(rich, spends)]
    print(f"  Segment {seg}: {name:<44} ({row['share']:>5} of customers, "
          f"${row['median_income']:,.0f}k income)")

         customers  median_income  median_spend  share
segment                                               
0               81           54.0          50.0  40.5%
1               39           79.0          83.0  19.5%
2               35           85.0          16.0  17.5%
3               23           25.0          17.0  11.5%
4               22           24.0          77.0  11.0%

Now name them, and say what to do:
  Segment 0: Budget-conscious — low priority              (40.5% of customers, $54k income)
  Segment 1: Best customers — reward and retain           (19.5% of customers, $79k income)
  Segment 2: Untapped — money, but not spending here      (17.5% of customers, $85k income)
  Segment 3: Budget-conscious — low priority              (11.5% of customers, $25k income)
  Segment 4: Enthusiasts on a budget — grow carefully     (11.0% of customers, $24k income)


That last block is the actual output of a clustering project. “Segment 1” became “high income, not spending — worth a targeted offer”, which somebody can act on tomorrow.

title: 12  Session 10 — Unsupervised Learning and Clustering
text:
16.1 8. Hierarchical clustering
Hierarchical clustering builds a tree. It starts with every point as its own cluster and repeatedly merges the two closest, until everything is one cluster. You then cut the tree wherever you like.
Its advantage over K-Means: you do not have to choose k in advance. You build the tree once and read off any number of clusters from it.

16.1.1 Demo 8 — the dendrogram

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import dendrogram, linkage, fcluster
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

sample = customers[["income", "spending_score"]].sample(40, random_state=1)
Z = linkage(StandardScaler().fit_transform(sample), method="ward")

plt.figure(figsize=(9, 3.4))
dendrogram(Z, no_labels=True)
plt.axhline(6, color="red", ls="--")
plt.ylabel("distance at which clusters merged")
plt.title("Cut the tree where the vertical lines are longest")
plt.show()

for cut in [2, 3, 4]:
    labels = fcluster(Z, cut, criterion="maxclust")
    print(f"cutting for {cut} clusters → sizes {np.bincount(labels)[1:].tolist()}")







Figure 16.1: A dendrogram. Cutting across at a height gives that many clusters — the long vertical gap suggests where.





cutting for 2 clusters → sizes [9, 31]
cutting for 3 clusters → sizes [9, 5, 26]
cutting for 4 clusters → sizes [9, 5, 5, 21]
crumbs: 12  Session 10 — Unsupervised Learning and Clustering

title: 12  Session 10 — Unsupervised Learning and Clustering
text:
16.2 9. DBSCAN
DBSCAN groups points that are packed closely together and labels everything else as noise. It has two strengths K-Means does not:

clusters can be any shape, not just round blobs
points that belong to no cluster are marked as noise rather than forced into one

You do not give it k. You give it eps (how close counts as “near”) and min_samples (how many neighbours make a dense region).

16.2.1 Demo 9 — the crescents, where K-Means could not win

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans, DBSCAN

mo = pd.read_csv("datasets/moons.csv")
moons, truth = mo[["x", "y"]].values, mo["true_group"].values

km_labels = KMeans(2, random_state=0, n_init=10).fit_predict(moons)
db_labels = DBSCAN(eps=0.2, min_samples=5).fit_predict(moons)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.2))
ax[0].scatter(*moons.T, c=truth, cmap="viridis", s=10);      ax[0].set_title("The truth")
ax[1].scatter(*moons.T, c=km_labels, cmap="viridis", s=10);  ax[1].set_title("K-Means")
ax[2].scatter(*moons.T, c=db_labels, cmap="viridis", s=10);  ax[2].set_title("DBSCAN")
for a in ax: a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

km_acc = max((km_labels == truth).mean(), 1 - (km_labels == truth).mean())
db_acc = max((db_labels == truth).mean(), 1 - (db_labels == truth).mean())
print(f"K-Means matches the true crescents: {km_acc:.0%}")
print(f"DBSCAN  matches the true crescents: {db_acc:.0%}")
print(f"DBSCAN labelled {(db_labels == -1).sum()} points as noise (label -1)")







Figure 16.2: K-Means cuts the crescents with a straight line. DBSCAN follows their shape.





K-Means matches the true crescents: 76%
DBSCAN  matches the true crescents: 100%
DBSCAN labelled 0 points as noise (label -1)




16.2.2 Demo 10 — choosing between the three

print(f"{'':<22} {'K-Means':<22} {'Hierarchical':<22} {'DBSCAN'}")
rows = [
    ("must choose k?",     "yes",                 "no — cut the tree",   "no"),
    ("cluster shapes",     "round blobs only",    "flexible",            "any shape"),
    ("handles noise",      "no — forces a group", "no",                  "yes, explicitly"),
    ("speed on big data",  "fast",                "slow (n² memory)",    "medium"),
    ("clusters of very different density", "poor", "fair",               "poor"),
    ("main use",           "the default first try","exploring structure","odd shapes, outliers"),
]
for label, a, b, c in rows:
    print(f"{label:<22} {a:<22} {b:<22} {c}")

                       K-Means                Hierarchical           DBSCAN
must choose k?         yes                    no — cut the tree      no
cluster shapes         round blobs only       flexible               any shape
handles noise          no — forces a group    no                     yes, explicitly
speed on big data      fast                   slow (n² memory)       medium
clusters of very different density poor                   fair                   poor
main use               the default first try  exploring structure    odd shapes, outliers




16.2.3 ❓ Check yourself
Q1. What makes clustering unsupervised?


It is less accurate.


There is no target column, so there is no correct answer to compare against.


It runs without training.


Q2. Why does inertia always fall as k rises?


A bug in scikit-learn.


More centres means every point is nearer to one, until with one centre per point inertia is zero.


It does not.


Q3. You cluster income (in rupees) and age (in years) without scaling. What happens?


Nothing important.


Income decides every cluster, because its numbers are thousands of times larger.


The code raises an error.


Q4. Your data forms two interlocking crescents. Which method?


K-Means with k=2.


DBSCAN.


K-Means with k=4.


Q5. The silhouette score for your clustering is 0.61, and the business says the segments make no sense. What do you conclude?


The business is wrong; 0.61 is a good score.


The clusters are mathematically separated but not meaningful — go back and change the features, not the score.


Increase k until the score improves.








NoteAnswers





A1 — (b). Which is why this chapter measures justification rather than accuracy.
A2 — (b). This is exactly why the elbow method looks for a bend rather than a minimum.
A3 — (b). Demo 3 measured 43% of applicants changing group on real loan data.
A4 — (b). Demo 9 measured K-Means at 76% and DBSCAN at essentially perfect.
A5 — (b). Demo 6’s noise experiment gave respectable silhouette scores on data with no structure at all. The score cannot tell you whether a grouping is meaningful.

title: 13  Session 11 — Model Evaluation
text:
