title: 13  Session 11 — Model Evaluation
text:
13.2 How this chapter is organised



Part
Question it answers




A — The two failures
What are the ways a model goes wrong?


B — Validation strategies
How do I get a score I can trust?


C — Evaluating with pictures
What does the score not tell me?


D — Tuning
How do I improve it without cheating?

title: 13  Session 11 — Model Evaluation
text:
14.1 1. Overfitting and underfitting
A model can fail in two opposite directions.









Underfitting
Overfitting




The model is
too simple
too complex


Training score
poor
excellent


Test score
poor
poor


It has
missed the pattern
memorised the noise


Fix by
adding features, using a richer model
simplifying, adding data, regularising



The diagnosis is the gap. Poor on both means underfitting. Excellent on training and poor on test means overfitting.






Tip🧠 Analogy — three students revising




The underfitting student skimmed one page. They do badly on the practice papers and badly in the exam.
The overfitting student memorised every practice paper word for word. Perfect on practice, lost in the exam when the questions are worded differently.
The good student learned the method. Slightly imperfect on practice, and fine in the exam.

Only the exam tells them apart — which is why the test set must stay sealed.



14.1.1 Demo 1 — watching a model overfit, in one table

import numpy as np
from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures, StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score

import pandas as pd

line = pd.read_csv("datasets/noisy_line.csv")   # 40 points on a noisy straight line
x, y = line["x"].values, line["y"].values

Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(x.reshape(-1, 1), y, test_size=.35, random_state=0)

print(f"{'model':<14} {'train R²':>9} {'test R²':>11}   verdict")
print("-" * 52)
for degree in [1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 12, 16]:
    # StandardScaler between the two steps keeps high powers numerically stable
    m = make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(degree), StandardScaler(), LinearRegression()).fit(Xtr, ytr)
    tr, te = r2_score(ytr, m.predict(Xtr)), r2_score(yte, m.predict(Xte))
    verdict = "OVERFITTING" if tr - te > 0.2 else "reasonable"
    print(f"degree {degree:<7} {tr:>9.3f} {te:>11.3f}   {verdict}")

model           train R²     test R²   verdict
----------------------------------------------------
degree 1           0.640       0.767   reasonable
degree 2           0.643       0.746   reasonable
degree 3           0.647       0.717   reasonable
degree 5           0.666       0.796   reasonable
degree 8           0.707      -2.975   OVERFITTING
degree 12          0.722     -44.941   OVERFITTING
degree 16          0.717    -187.128   OVERFITTING


Watch the two columns separate. Training R² climbs steadily as the model is given more freedom — it can always bend closer to points it has already seen. The test score peaks around degree 5 and then falls off a cliff: −45 at degree 12, −187 at degree 16.
A negative R² means worse than always guessing the average. The degree-16 model fits its training data better than any other model in the table and is, on unseen data, far worse than useless.


14.1.2 Demo 2 — the same thing as a picture

import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

grid = np.linspace(0, 10, 300).reshape(-1, 1)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.2))
for ax, degree in zip(axes, [1, 3, 14]):
    m = make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(degree), LinearRegression()).fit(Xtr, ytr)
    ax.scatter(Xtr, ytr, s=18, label="training")
    ax.scatter(Xte, yte, s=18, color="orange", label="test")
    ax.plot(grid, m.predict(grid), "r-", lw=1.8)
    ax.set_ylim(y.min()-6, y.max()+6)
    ax.set_title(f"degree {degree}", fontsize=10)
axes[0].legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print("Degree 14 passes almost exactly through the blue training points — and swings")
print("wildly between them, which is where the orange test points live.")







Figure 14.1: Degree 1 misses the pattern. Degree 14 passes through every training point and is useless between them.





Degree 14 passes almost exactly through the blue training points — and swings
wildly between them, which is where the orange test points live.

title: 13  Session 11 — Model Evaluation
text:
14.2 2. Bias and variance
These are the technical names for the two failures.








Term
Means
Shows up as




Bias
error from wrong assumptions — the model is too simple to represent the truth
underfitting


Variance
error from sensitivity to the particular training data
overfitting



The trade-off: making a model more flexible reduces bias and increases variance. There is a middle point, and finding it is what the rest of this chapter is for.

14.2.1 Demo 3 — variance made visible

import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

import pandas as pd

samples = pd.read_csv("datasets/repeated_samples.csv")   # six draws from the same truth
grid = np.linspace(0, 10, 200).reshape(-1, 1)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.3))
for degree, a in zip([1, 12], ax):
    for sample_id, g in samples.groupby("sample"):
        xs, ys = g["x"].values, g["y"].values
        m = make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(degree), LinearRegression()).fit(xs.reshape(-1,1), ys)
        a.plot(grid, m.predict(grid), lw=1.2, alpha=.8)
    a.set_ylim(-10, 30); a.set_title(f"degree {degree}: {'low' if degree==1 else 'high'} variance")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print("Left: six nearly identical lines — low variance, the model is stable.")
print("Right: six wildly different curves from the same underlying truth —")
print("       high variance. Which one you get depends on which rows you happened to draw.")







Figure 14.2: The same model fitted to six different samples from the same source. The flexible model changes shape wildly; the simple one barely moves.





Left: six nearly identical lines — low variance, the model is stable.
Right: six wildly different curves from the same underlying truth —
       high variance. Which one you get depends on which rows you happened to draw.

title: 13  Session 11 — Model Evaluation
section: 15.1 3. Why one split is not enough
text:
15.1 3. Why one split is not enough
A single train–test split gives you one number, and that number depends on which rows happened to land in the test set.

15.1.1 Demo 4 — the same model, twenty different scores

import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score

feats = pd.read_csv("datasets/three_features.csv")
X = feats[["f1", "f2", "f3"]].values
y = feats["target"].values

scores = []
for seed in range(20):
    Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=.3, random_state=seed)
    scores.append(r2_score(yte, LinearRegression().fit(Xtr, ytr).predict(Xte)))

scores = np.array(scores)
print(f"lowest  R² : {scores.min():.3f}")
print(f"highest R² : {scores.max():.3f}")
print(f"spread     : {scores.max()-scores.min():.3f}")
print(f"average    : {scores.mean():.3f}  (± {scores.std():.3f})")
print("\nSame model, same data, same code. Only the random seed changed.")

lowest  R² : 0.556
highest R² : 0.795
spread     : 0.239
average    : 0.695  (± 0.063)

Same model, same data, same code. Only the random seed changed.








Warning⚠️ Report a range, not a point



If your model scores 0.71 and a colleague’s scores 0.74, and single splits vary by 0.15, you have not shown that yours is worse. You have shown two draws from overlapping ranges.
Any comparison of two models must use the same folds and account for the spread.

title: 13  Session 11 — Model Evaluation
text:
15.2 4. K-fold cross-validation
Cross-validation splits the data into k parts, then trains k times — each time holding out a different part for testing. Every row is used for testing exactly once.





flowchart TB
    D["all training data, split into 5 folds"]
    D --> R1["run 1: test on fold 1, train on 2,3,4,5"]
    D --> R2["run 2: test on fold 2, train on 1,3,4,5"]
    D --> R3["run 3: test on fold 3, train on 1,2,4,5"]
    D --> R4["run 4: test on fold 4, train on 1,2,3,5"]
    D --> R5["run 5: test on fold 5, train on 1,2,3,4"]
    R1 --> A["average the 5 scores<br/><b>and report the spread</b>"]
    R2 --> A
    R3 --> A
    R4 --> A
    R5 --> A







15.2.1 Demo 5 — cross-validation, fold by fold

import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, KFold

cv = KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
fold_scores = cross_val_score(LinearRegression(), X, y, cv=cv, scoring="r2")

for i, s in enumerate(fold_scores, 1):
    print(f"  fold {i}: R² = {s:.3f}")
print(f"\nreport this: R² = {fold_scores.mean():.3f} ± {fold_scores.std():.3f}")
print(f"a single split could have given you anything from {fold_scores.min():.3f} "
      f"to {fold_scores.max():.3f}")

  fold 1: R² = 0.703
  fold 2: R² = 0.802
  fold 3: R² = 0.729
  fold 4: R² = 0.732
  fold 5: R² = 0.656

report this: R² = 0.724 ± 0.047
a single split could have given you anything from 0.656 to 0.802

title: 13  Session 11 — Model Evaluation
text:
15.3 5. Choosing a validation strategy

print(f"{'strategy':<24} {'how it works':<44} {'use when'}")
print("-" * 108)
rows = [
    ("Holdout",           "one split, e.g. 80/20",                      "data is huge; you need a quick answer"),
    ("K-fold",            "k splits, every row tested once",            "the default"),
    ("Stratified k-fold", "k-fold keeping class proportions",           "classification, especially imbalanced"),
    ("Leave-one-out",     "k = number of rows",                         "very small datasets; expensive"),
    ("Bootstrapping",     "sample with replacement, many times",        "you want a confidence interval"),
    ("Time-series split", "always train on the past, test on the future","the rows are ordered in time"),
]
for r in rows:
    print(f"{r[0]:<24} {r[1]:<44} {r[2]}")

strategy                 how it works                                 use when
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Holdout                  one split, e.g. 80/20                        data is huge; you need a quick answer
K-fold                   k splits, every row tested once              the default
Stratified k-fold        k-fold keeping class proportions             classification, especially imbalanced
Leave-one-out            k = number of rows                           very small datasets; expensive
Bootstrapping            sample with replacement, many times          you want a confidence interval
Time-series split        always train on the past, test on the future the rows are ordered in time








Warning⚠️ Never shuffle time-ordered data



Ordinary k-fold shuffles rows, so a model can be trained on next month and tested on last month. It will look excellent and be worthless, because in production the future is not available. For anything with a time order, use TimeSeriesSplit.



15.3.1 Demo 6 — bootstrapping for a confidence interval

import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score

rng = np.random.default_rng(54)
boot_scores = []
for _ in range(500):
    idx = rng.integers(0, len(X), len(X))               # sample rows WITH replacement
    oob = np.setdiff1d(np.arange(len(X)), idx)          # rows not drawn = the test set
    if len(oob) < 5:
        continue
    m = LinearRegression().fit(X[idx], y[idx])
    boot_scores.append(r2_score(y[oob], m.predict(X[oob])))

lo, hi = np.percentile(boot_scores, [2.5, 97.5])
print(f"bootstrap estimate of R²: {np.mean(boot_scores):.3f}")
print(f"95% confidence interval : {lo:.3f} to {hi:.3f}")
print(f"\nBased on {len(boot_scores)} resamples. Quote the interval, not the point.")

bootstrap estimate of R²: 0.705
95% confidence interval : 0.562 to 0.802

Based on 500 resamples. Quote the interval, not the point.

title: 13  Session 11 — Model Evaluation
section: 16.1 6. What a score cannot tell you
text:
16.1 6. What a score cannot tell you
A single number compresses every mistake into one figure, and hides where the mistakes are. Two models with identical R² can be wrong in completely different ways.

16.1.1 Demo 7 — the residual plot

import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

import pandas as pd

rc = pd.read_csv("datasets/residual_cases.csv")
xs = rc["x"].values
cases = {
    "Healthy":         rc["healthy"].values,
    "Missing a curve": rc["curved"].values,
    "Growing error":   rc["growing_error"].values,
}

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.2))
for ax, (name, yy) in zip(axes, cases.items()):
    m = LinearRegression().fit(xs.reshape(-1,1), yy)
    pred = m.predict(xs.reshape(-1,1))
    ax.scatter(pred, yy - pred, s=9, alpha=.6)
    ax.axhline(0, color="red", lw=1.5)
    ax.set_title(f"{name}\nR² = {m.score(xs.reshape(-1,1), yy):.3f}", fontsize=9)
    ax.set_xlabel("predicted"); ax.set_ylabel("residual")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print("All three have a respectable R². Only the first is a model you should ship.")
print("  curve  → the relationship is not linear; the model is systematically wrong")
print("           at both ends and systematically right in the middle")
print("  fan    → the model is reliable for small predictions and unreliable for large")
print("           ones. A single R² averages those two very different situations.")







Figure 16.1: Predicted versus residual. A healthy model shows a shapeless band around zero.





All three have a respectable R². Only the first is a model you should ship.
  curve  → the relationship is not linear; the model is systematically wrong
           at both ends and systematically right in the middle
  fan    → the model is reliable for small predictions and unreliable for large
           ones. A single R² averages those two very different situations.

title: 13  Session 11 — Model Evaluation
text:
16.2 7. The distribution of the errors
Plotting the errors themselves shows whether the model is biased and how bad the worst cases are.

16.2.1 Demo 8 — the error distribution, and what it reveals

import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

shapes = pd.read_csv("datasets/error_shapes.csv")
Xa = shapes[["f1", "f2"]].values
good_y = shapes["target_normal"].values
skew_y = shapes["target_heavy"].values     # heavy tails: rare, very large errors

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.2))
for a, (name, yy) in zip(ax, [("Healthy errors", good_y), ("Heavy-tailed errors", skew_y)]):
    Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(Xa, yy, test_size=.3, random_state=0)
    err = yte - LinearRegression().fit(Xtr, ytr).predict(Xte)
    a.hist(err, bins=40); a.axvline(0, color="red")
    a.set_title(f"{name}\nmean error {err.mean():+.2f}, worst {np.abs(err).max():.1f}", fontsize=9)
    a.set_xlabel("error")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print("Both models have a mean error near zero — they are unbiased on average.")
print("The right-hand one still has occasional predictions that are badly wrong.")
print("If a single bad prediction is expensive, the average was never the right measure.")







Figure 16.2: Left: errors centred on zero and symmetric — healthy. Right: a long tail, so a few predictions are badly wrong.





Both models have a mean error near zero — they are unbiased on average.
The right-hand one still has occasional predictions that are badly wrong.
If a single bad prediction is expensive, the average was never the right measure.




16.2.2 Demo 9 — predicted versus actual

import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(Xa, good_y, test_size=.3, random_state=0)
pred = LinearRegression().fit(Xtr, ytr).predict(Xte)

plt.scatter(yte, pred, s=12, alpha=.6)
lims = [min(yte.min(), pred.min()), max(yte.max(), pred.max())]
plt.plot(lims, lims, "r--", lw=1.5, label="perfect prediction")
plt.xlabel("actual"); plt.ylabel("predicted"); plt.legend()
plt.show()

print("Points above the line: the model predicted too high. Below: too low.")
print("A systematic tilt away from the diagonal means the model is biased at one end.")







Figure 16.3: Predicted against actual. Perfect predictions lie on the diagonal.





Points above the line: the model predicted too high. Below: too low.
A systematic tilt away from the diagonal means the model is biased at one end.

title: 13  Session 11 — Model Evaluation
text:
16.3 8. Learning curves
A learning curve shows the score as training data increases. It tells you what to do next.

16.3.1 Demo 10 — “get more data” or “get a better model”?

import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.model_selection import learning_curve
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor

curved = pd.read_csv("datasets/curved_truth.csv")      # the truth here is a curve
Xb = curved[["f1", "f2"]].values
yb = curved["target"].values

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.3))
for a, (name, model) in zip(ax, [("Too simple (linear)", LinearRegression()),
                                 ("Flexible (deep tree)", DecisionTreeRegressor(random_state=0))]):
    sizes, train_s, val_s = learning_curve(model, Xb, yb, cv=5,
                                           train_sizes=np.linspace(.1, 1, 8), scoring="r2")
    a.plot(sizes, train_s.mean(1), "o-", label="training score")
    a.plot(sizes, val_s.mean(1), "o-", label="validation score")
    a.set_title(name, fontsize=10); a.set_xlabel("training rows"); a.set_ylim(-.1, 1.05)
    a.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print("LEFT — both curves flat and low, sitting on top of each other:")
print("       the model is too simple. More data changes nothing. Change the model.")
print("RIGHT — a gap between the curves that is still narrowing:")
print("       the model is learning. More data would still help.")







Figure 16.4: Left: the curves converge at a poor score — more data will not help. Right: a gap that is still closing — more data will help.





LEFT — both curves flat and low, sitting on top of each other:
       the model is too simple. More data changes nothing. Change the model.
RIGHT — a gap between the curves that is still narrowing:
       the model is learning. More data would still help.

title: 13  Session 11 — Model Evaluation
text:
17.1 9. Hyperparameters
A hyperparameter is a setting you choose before training — the depth of a tree, the k in k-Nearest Neighbours, the strength of a regularisation penalty. The model learns its coefficients; it does not learn these.








Method
How it searches
Use when




Grid search
every combination you list
few settings, small ranges


Random search
random combinations, a fixed budget
many settings — usually beats grid for the same cost


Bayesian optimisation
uses past results to choose what to try next
training is expensive




17.1.1 Demo 11 — grid search, done correctly

import numpy as np
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score

Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(Xb, yb, test_size=.25, random_state=0)

grid = GridSearchCV(
    DecisionTreeRegressor(random_state=0),
    param_grid={"max_depth": [2, 3, 5, 8, 12, None],
                "min_samples_leaf": [1, 5, 20]},
    cv=5, scoring="r2",
)
grid.fit(Xtr, ytr)          # note: only the TRAINING data goes in here

print(f"combinations tried : {len(grid.cv_results_['params'])}")
print(f"best settings      : {grid.best_params_}")
print(f"best CV score      : {grid.best_score_:.3f}   (measured on the training folds)")
print(f"score on the sealed test set: {r2_score(yte, grid.predict(Xte)):.3f}")

combinations tried : 18
best settings      : {'max_depth': 12, 'min_samples_leaf': 1}
best CV score      : 0.944   (measured on the training folds)
score on the sealed test set: 0.945


The test set was used exactly once, at the very end. The search compared 18 combinations using cross-validation inside the training data.


17.1.2 Demo 12 — what tuning on the test set does
The damage from peeking is selection bias: when you try many candidates and keep the one that scored highest, the score you kept is partly a measure of luck. Here the signal is genuinely weak, so the candidates are nearly equivalent and “best” is mostly noise — which is exactly the situation where peeking hurts most.

import numpy as np
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score

weak = pd.read_csv("datasets/weak_signal.csv")   # one real driver, buried in noise
Xw = weak[[f"f{i}" for i in range(1, 7)]].values
yw = weak["target"].values

Xtr, Xtmp, ytr, ytmp = train_test_split(Xw, yw, test_size=.4, random_state=0)
Xpeek, Xfresh, ypeek, yfresh = train_test_split(Xtmp, ytmp, test_size=.5, random_state=1)

candidates = [(d, leaf) for d in [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 12, None]
                        for leaf in [1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 40, 80]]

def score_on(Xset, yset, depth, leaf):
    m = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=depth, min_samples_leaf=leaf, random_state=0)
    return r2_score(yset, m.fit(Xtr, ytr).predict(Xset))

peeked = {c: score_on(Xpeek, ypeek, *c) for c in candidates}
best = max(peeked, key=peeked.get)

print(f"settings tried            : {len(candidates)}")
print(f"best score while peeking  : {peeked[best]:+.3f}   (max_depth={best[0]}, min_samples_leaf={best[1]})")
print(f"that same model, fresh data: {score_on(Xfresh, yfresh, *best):+.3f}")
print(f"\nflattery                  : {peeked[best] - score_on(Xfresh, yfresh, *best):+.3f}")
print(f"average candidate, peek set : {np.mean(list(peeked.values())):+.3f}")

settings tried            : 56
best score while peeking  : +0.084   (max_depth=2, min_samples_leaf=80)
that same model, fresh data: -0.204

flattery                  : +0.288
average candidate, peek set : -0.189


The reported figure was positive. The truth was negative. Nothing about that model was good — it was simply the luckiest of 56 draws against one small set of rows, and the score that made it look best was the part that would not repeat.
Note that the average candidate scored badly on the peek set too. The problem is not that the models were good and got worse; it is that taking the maximum over many noisy measurements returns an inflated measurement.






Important🔓 The test set is spent after one use



Every time you look at the test score and change something because of it, you leak a little information into your choices. Do it twenty times and the test set has quietly become a second training set.
The discipline:

Split off the test set and do not touch it
Do all tuning with cross-validation on the training data
Look at the test set once, at the very end, and report what it says
If you then change the model, you need a fresh test set





17.1.3 Demo 13 — the whole evaluation, as one report

import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.dummy import DummyRegressor
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, KFold, train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, r2_score

Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(Xb, yb, test_size=.25, random_state=0)
cv = KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)

for name, model in [("Baseline (mean)", DummyRegressor()),
                    ("Linear regression", LinearRegression()),
                    ("Random forest", RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=120, random_state=0))]:
    folds = cross_val_score(model, Xtr, ytr, cv=cv, scoring="r2")
    model.fit(Xtr, ytr)
    pred = model.predict(Xte)
    print(f"{name:<20} CV R² {folds.mean():>6.3f} ± {folds.std():.3f}   "
          f"test R² {r2_score(yte, pred):>6.3f}   test MAE {mean_absolute_error(yte, pred):>5.2f}")

print("\nThe forest wins, and the ± tells you the win is larger than the fold-to-fold noise.")

Baseline (mean)      CV R² -0.010 ± 0.009   test R² -0.000   test MAE  3.02
Linear regression    CV R²  0.375 ± 0.053   test R²  0.514   test MAE  2.06
Random forest        CV R²  0.972 ± 0.006   test R²  0.969   test MAE  0.47

The forest wins, and the ± tells you the win is larger than the fold-to-fold noise.




17.1.4 ❓ Check yourself
Q1. Training R² is 0.99, test R² is 0.41. What is happening?


Underfitting.


Overfitting.


The model is good.


Q2. Both scores are around 0.3. What should you do?


Simplify the model.


Use a richer model or add better features — it is underfitting.


Collect more rows.


Q3. Why report R² as 0.71 ± 0.06 rather than 0.71?


It looks more professional.


A single split can vary by more than the difference you are trying to detect.


R² is always uncertain.


Q4. Your data is monthly sales for five years. Which validation?


K-fold with shuffling.


TimeSeriesSplit — always train on earlier months, test on later ones.


Leave-one-out.


Q5. You tried 30 model settings, kept the one with the best test score, and reported that score. What is wrong?


30 is too many.


The test set was used to make a choice, so the reported score is optimistic. It is no longer an unbiased estimate.


Nothing.








NoteAnswers





A1 — (b). Excellent on seen data, poor on unseen data — Demo 1’s right-hand column.
A2 — (b). Poor on both is the underfitting signature. Demo 10’s left panel shows what the learning curve looks like.
A3 — (b). Demo 4 measured a spread of over 0.15 across seeds on the same model.
A4 — (b). Shuffling lets the model train on the future. It will look excellent and be worthless.
A5 — (b). Demo 12 measured exactly this gap.

title: 14  Session 12 — Model Saving and Deployment
section: 15.1 1. Why a trained model has to be saved
text:
15.1 1. Why a trained model has to be saved
Training happens once; predicting happens thousands of times. Retraining a model every time somebody asks a question would be slow, expensive, and would give slightly different answers each run.
So the trained model is written to a file. That file contains the learned numbers — coefficients, tree splits, the scaler’s mean — and can be loaded in milliseconds.






Tip🧠 Analogy — the recipe and the cooking



Working out a recipe takes weeks of experimenting. Cooking from it takes twenty minutes.
Training is developing the recipe. Saving is writing it down. Prediction is cooking. You do not redevelop the recipe every time somebody orders dinner.
crumbs: 14  Session 12 — Model Saving and Deployment

title: 14  Session 12 — Model Saving and Deployment
section: 15.2 2. Save the pipeline, not the model
text:
15.2 2. Save the pipeline, not the model
This is the mistake that costs the most and announces itself the least.
A trained LinearRegression knows its coefficients. It does not know that its inputs were scaled before training. Feed it raw, unscaled numbers and it will apply coefficients meant for scaled ones — and return a number, confidently, with no error.

15.2.1 Demo 1 — the silent failure, measured

import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

homes = pd.read_csv("datasets/house_prices_simple.csv")
print(f"{len(homes)} houses on file: {list(homes.columns)}\n")

X = homes[["area_sqft", "age_years"]]
y = homes["price"]
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=.2, random_state=0)

# Train with scaling, as Session 5 taught.
scaler = StandardScaler().fit(X_train)
model = LinearRegression().fit(scaler.transform(X_train), y_train)

new_house = pd.DataFrame([{"area_sqft": 1500, "age_years": 5}])

right = model.predict(scaler.transform(new_house))[0]     # scaled, as trained
wrong = model.predict(new_house)[0]                       # raw — the bug

print(f"Correct  (scaled input) : ₹{right:>15,.0f}")
print(f"Bug      (raw input)    : ₹{wrong:>15,.0f}")
print(f"\nNo error was raised. The wrong answer is off by ₹{abs(right-wrong):,.0f}.")

500 houses on file: ['area_sqft', 'age_years', 'price']

Correct  (scaled input) : ₹      4,994,176
Bug      (raw input)    : ₹  1,694,069,949

No error was raised. The wrong answer is off by ₹1,689,075,773.


Both lines ran without complaint. In a web app, the second would be shown to a user as a house valuation.


15.2.2 Demo 2 — the fix: one object that carries everything

from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline

pipeline = Pipeline([
    ("scale", StandardScaler()),
    ("model", LinearRegression()),
]).fit(X_train, y_train)

print(f"Pipeline on raw input   : ₹{pipeline.predict(new_house)[0]:>15,.0f}")
print(f"Correct answer from above: ₹{right:>15,.0f}")
print("\nThe pipeline takes RAW input and scales it internally. There is no way")
print("to forget the scaler, because the scaler is inside the thing you saved.")

Pipeline on raw input   : ₹      4,994,176
Correct answer from above: ₹      4,994,176

The pipeline takes RAW input and scales it internally. There is no way
to forget the scaler, because the scaler is inside the thing you saved.

title: 14  Session 12 — Model Saving and Deployment
text:
15.3 3. Saving and loading
joblib writes a fitted Python object to a file and reads it back. It is preferred over pickle for scikit-learn because it stores large numeric arrays more efficiently.

15.3.1 Demo 3 — a full save-and-reload round trip

import joblib, tempfile, os
import numpy as np

folder = tempfile.mkdtemp()
path = os.path.join(folder, "house_price_pipeline.joblib")

joblib.dump(pipeline, path)
print(f"saved to {os.path.basename(path)}  ({os.path.getsize(path):,} bytes)")

loaded = joblib.load(path)
print(f"loaded back: {type(loaded).__name__} with steps {[n for n, _ in loaded.steps]}")

before = pipeline.predict(X_test)
after   = loaded.predict(X_test)
print(f"\npredictions identical after reload: {np.allclose(before, after)}")
print(f"largest difference: {np.abs(before - after).max():.10f}")

saved to house_price_pipeline.joblib  (1,361 bytes)
loaded back: Pipeline with steps ['scale', 'model']

predictions identical after reload: True
largest difference: 0.0000000000




15.3.2 Demo 4 — save everything needed to reproduce the model

import joblib, sklearn, os, json
from datetime import date
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, r2_score

bundle = {
    "pipeline": pipeline,
    "feature_names": list(X.columns),           # so the app builds rows in the right order
    "target": "price",
    "trained_on": str(date.today()),
    "n_training_rows": len(X_train),
    "sklearn_version": sklearn.__version__,
    "test_mae": float(mean_absolute_error(y_test, pipeline.predict(X_test))),
    "test_r2": float(r2_score(y_test, pipeline.predict(X_test))),
}

bundle_path = os.path.join(folder, "model_bundle.joblib")
joblib.dump(bundle, bundle_path)

back = joblib.load(bundle_path)
print(json.dumps({k: v for k, v in back.items() if k != "pipeline"}, indent=2))

{
  "feature_names": [
    "area_sqft",
    "age_years"
  ],
  "target": "price",
  "trained_on": "2026-09-11",
  "n_training_rows": 400,
  "sklearn_version": "1.9.0",
  "test_mae": 169824.38561731137,
  "test_r2": 0.9679916797170471
}


Everything except the pipeline itself is metadata, and every field earns its place:







Field
Answers




feature_names
what order do the columns go in?


sklearn_version
why does this behave differently now?


test_mae, test_r2
is the live model still as good as when we shipped it?


trained_on
how stale is this?









Warning⚠️ A saved model is tied to its library version



A pipeline saved under scikit-learn 1.3 and loaded under 1.5 may warn, may behave differently, or may refuse to load. Pin your versions in requirements.txt and record the version in the bundle so the mismatch is diagnosable rather than mysterious.



print("requirements.txt should pin exactly what trained the model, for example:")
print(f"  scikit-learn=={sklearn.__version__}")
print(f"  pandas=={pd.__version__}")
print(f"  numpy=={np.__version__}")

requirements.txt should pin exactly what trained the model, for example:
  scikit-learn==1.9.0
  pandas==3.0.5
  numpy==2.4.6

text:
16.1 4. One inference function
Write one function that turns raw user input into a prediction, and use it everywhere — the notebook, the app, the batch job, the tests. If the app builds its input rows differently from the notebook, you have two models.

16.1.1 Demo 5 — predict_one, with input validation

import pandas as pd, joblib

def load_model(path):
    b = joblib.load(path)
    return b["pipeline"], b["feature_names"]

def predict_price(area_sqft, age_years, model_path=bundle_path):
    """Turn raw user input into a price. Validates before predicting."""
    if not 200 <= area_sqft <= 10_000:
        raise ValueError(f"area_sqft {area_sqft} is outside the sensible range 200–10,000")
    if not 0 <= age_years <= 120:
        raise ValueError(f"age_years {age_years} is outside the sensible range 0–120")

    pipe, features = load_model(model_path)
    row = pd.DataFrame([{"area_sqft": area_sqft, "age_years": age_years}])[features]
    return float(pipe.predict(row)[0])

for area, age in [(800, 2), (1500, 5), (2400, 20)]:
    print(f"{area:>5} sqft, {age:>2} years old → ₹{predict_price(area, age):>12,.0f}")

try:
    predict_price(-50, 5)
except ValueError as e:
    print(f"\nRejected bad input: {e}")

  800 sqft,  2 years old → ₹   2,878,291
 1500 sqft,  5 years old → ₹   4,994,176
 2400 sqft, 20 years old → ₹   7,199,992

Rejected bad input: area_sqft -50 is outside the sensible range 200–10,000








Important🔓 Validate at the door



A model will happily predict a price for a house of −50 square feet. The model is not where you catch nonsense — the input layer is. Every deployed model needs a range check in front of it, because users type things.

title: 14  Session 12 — Model Saving and Deployment
text:
16.2 5. Offline and online deployment
There are two ways to deliver predictions, and the choice follows from when the answer is needed.









Offline (batch)
Online (live)




When it runs
on a schedule — nightly, weekly
the moment someone asks


Input
a whole file of rows
one row


Output
a table of predictions
one answer


Delivered as
a CSV, a database table, a dashboard
a web app or an API


Needs a server running?
no — a scheduled job
yes, always on


Cost
low
higher


Good for
churn scores, restock lists, risk ratings
loan decisions, fraud checks, search



Most projects should start offline. If a nightly file of predictions solves the problem, you have avoided servers, uptime and latency entirely.

16.2.1 Demo 6 — offline scoring, which is often the whole product

import pandas as pd, joblib, os

# A batch job: read the properties awaiting valuation, score them, write the file, stop.
portfolio = pd.read_csv("datasets/property_portfolio.csv")

pipe, features = load_model(bundle_path)
portfolio["estimated_price"] = pipe.predict(portfolio[features]).round(-3)
portfolio["price_per_sqft"] = (portfolio["estimated_price"] / portfolio["area_sqft"]).round(0)

print(portfolio.to_string(index=False))

out = os.path.join(folder, "valuations.csv")
portfolio.to_csv(out, index=False)
print(f"\nwritten to {os.path.basename(out)} — this file is the deliverable")

property_id  area_sqft  age_years  estimated_price  price_per_sqft
      P0001        900         12        2739000.0          3043.0
      P0002       1250          3        4281000.0          3425.0
      P0003       1800         25        5037000.0          2798.0
      P0004        640         40         608000.0           950.0
      P0005       2200          1        7433000.0          3379.0
      P0006       1500          8        4856000.0          3237.0
      P0007       1050         18        2945000.0          2805.0
      P0008       3000          5        9825000.0          3275.0

written to valuations.csv — this file is the deliverable




16.2.2 Demo 7 — online scoring, one request at a time

import time, joblib

pipe, features = load_model(bundle_path)          # load ONCE, not per request

def handle_request(payload: dict) -> dict:
    """What a web endpoint does for a single incoming request."""
    start = time.perf_counter()
    row = pd.DataFrame([payload])[features]
    price = float(pipe.predict(row)[0])
    return {
        "estimated_price": round(price, -3),
        "confidence_note": "typical error ±₹{:,.0f}".format(joblib.load(bundle_path)["test_mae"]),
        "latency_ms": round((time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000, 2),
    }

for payload in [{"area_sqft": 1500, "age_years": 5}, {"area_sqft": 2400, "age_years": 20}]:
    print(payload, "→", handle_request(payload))

{'area_sqft': 1500, 'age_years': 5} → {'estimated_price': 4994000.0, 'confidence_note': 'typical error ±₹169,824', 'latency_ms': 1.29}
{'area_sqft': 2400, 'age_years': 20} → {'estimated_price': 7200000.0, 'confidence_note': 'typical error ±₹169,824', 'latency_ms': 1.12}


Note where the model is loaded. Loading it inside the request function would reread the file on every call. Loading it once, when the process starts, is the difference between a page that responds instantly and one that does not.

text:
17.1 6. What Streamlit does
Streamlit turns a Python script into a web page. There is no HTML, no JavaScript and no web framework to learn: you write st.slider(...) and a slider appears.
Every Streamlit app is the same four steps:







Step
Code




1. Load the model once
@st.cache_resource + joblib.load


2. Collect input from widgets
st.slider, st.number_input, st.selectbox


3. Predict
pipeline.predict(row)


4. Show the answer
st.metric, st.write

title: 14  Session 12 — Model Saving and Deployment
text:
17.2 7. The app
The code below is a complete, working application. It is shown rather than run, because a Streamlit app needs a web server — the cells in this book run in a notebook kernel. Save it as app.py and run streamlit run app.py.
# app.py — a complete house price estimator
import streamlit as st
import pandas as pd
import joblib

st.set_page_config(page_title="House price estimator", page_icon="🏠")

# --- STEP 1: load the model ONCE, not on every interaction -----------------
@st.cache_resource
def load_bundle():
    return joblib.load("model_bundle.joblib")

bundle = load_bundle()
pipeline = bundle["pipeline"]
features = bundle["feature_names"]

# --- STEP 2: collect input -------------------------------------------------
st.title("🏠 House price estimator")
st.caption(f"Model trained {bundle['trained_on']} on {bundle['n_training_rows']:,} properties")

col1, col2 = st.columns(2)
with col1:
    area = st.slider("Floor area (sq ft)", 400, 3000, 1200, step=50)
with col2:
    age = st.slider("Age of property (years)", 0, 40, 5)

# --- STEP 3: predict -------------------------------------------------------
row = pd.DataFrame([{"area_sqft": area, "age_years": age}])[features]
price = float(pipeline.predict(row)[0])

# --- STEP 4: show the answer, with its uncertainty -------------------------
st.metric("Estimated price", f"₹{price:,.0f}")
st.caption(f"Typical error on unseen properties: ±₹{bundle['test_mae']:,.0f}")

with st.expander("How reliable is this?"):
    st.write(f"""
    - Test R²: **{bundle['test_r2']:.2f}** — the share of price variation the model explains
    - Trained on properties between 400 and 3,000 sq ft. Estimates outside that
      range are extrapolation and should not be relied on.
    - This is a statistical estimate, not a valuation.
    """)






Warning⚠️ @st.cache_resource is not optional



Without it, Streamlit reruns the entire script every time a slider moves — including joblib.load. On a large model that is a visible freeze on every interaction. @st.cache_resource loads it once and keeps it.



17.2.1 Demo 8 — the app’s logic, tested without a browser
You can and should test the prediction logic directly. Everything except the widgets is ordinary Python.

import pandas as pd, joblib

bundle = joblib.load(bundle_path)
pipe, features = bundle["pipeline"], bundle["feature_names"]

def app_logic(area, age):
    row = pd.DataFrame([{"area_sqft": area, "age_years": age}])[features]
    return float(pipe.predict(row)[0])

print(f"{'area':>6} {'age':>4} {'estimate':>16}")
for area in [600, 1200, 2000]:
    for age in [0, 20]:
        print(f"{area:>6} {age:>4} ₹{app_logic(area, age):>15,.0f}")

print(f"\nSanity checks the app should pass:")
print(f"  bigger house costs more     : {app_logic(2000, 5) > app_logic(1000, 5)}")
print(f"  older house costs less      : {app_logic(1500, 30) < app_logic(1500, 2)}")
print(f"  test MAE quoted to the user : ₹{bundle['test_mae']:,.0f}")

  area  age         estimate
   600    0 ₹      2,326,532
   600   20 ₹      1,402,877
  1200    0 ₹      4,258,904
  1200   20 ₹      3,335,249
  2000    0 ₹      6,835,400
  2000   20 ₹      5,911,744

title: 14  Session 12 — Model Saving and Deployment
text:
17.3 8. Publishing it
Streamlit Community Cloud hosts small apps free, straight from a GitHub repository.



Your repository needs
Why




app.py
the application


model_bundle.joblib
the trained pipeline, committed


requirements.txt
with versions pinned


README.md
what it does and what it must not be used for



Then: push to GitHub → connect the repository at share.streamlit.io → choose app.py → deploy.






Warning⚠️ Never commit secrets



API keys, database passwords and connection strings must not be in the repository, and must not be in the model bundle. Streamlit provides st.secrets for this. A key pushed to GitHub is compromised even if you delete it afterwards — the history keeps it.

title: 14  Session 12 — Model Saving and Deployment
text:
18.1 9. What breaks
A deployed model degrades even when nobody touches the code, because the world it learned from carries on changing.








Problem
What happens
How you notice




Data drift
inputs shift — house sizes, customer ages
monitor input distributions


Concept drift
the relationship shifts — a market crash
monitor live accuracy


Schema change
an upstream column is renamed or reformatted
the app crashes, or worse, silently misreads


Version drift
the library is upgraded under the model
pin versions; record them


Extrapolation
users enter values outside the training range
validate inputs




18.1.1 Demo 10 — detecting drift by watching the inputs

import numpy as np, pandas as pd

training_areas = X_train["area_sqft"]

# What the live service actually received, month by month.
incoming = pd.read_csv("datasets/incoming_requests.csv")
months = {m: g["area_sqft"].values for m, g in incoming.groupby("month")}

print(f"training data: mean {training_areas.mean():,.0f}, "
      f"Q1 {training_areas.quantile(.25):,.0f}, Q3 {training_areas.quantile(.75):,.0f}\n")

for name, seen in months.items():
    shift = (seen.mean() - training_areas.mean()) / training_areas.std()
    outside = ((seen < training_areas.min()) | (seen > training_areas.max())).mean()
    flag = "  ⚠ DRIFT — retrain" if abs(shift) > 0.5 else ""
    print(f"{name}: mean {seen.mean():>7,.0f}   shift {shift:+.2f} std   "
          f"{outside:>5.1%} outside training range{flag}")

training data: mean 1,184, Q1 953, Q3 1,418

Month 1: mean   1,189   shift +0.01 std    0.7% outside training range
Month 4: mean   1,259   shift +0.21 std    0.7% outside training range
Month 8: mean   1,695   shift +1.45 std    2.0% outside training range  ⚠ DRIFT — retrain


No accuracy figure was needed. Watching the inputs catches drift before the predictions have visibly gone wrong — and long before anybody complains.


18.1.2 Demo 11 — the deployment checklist, as code

import joblib, os

def preflight(bundle_path):
    """Checks to run before any model goes live."""
    b = joblib.load(bundle_path)
    checks = {
        "pipeline saved (not a bare model)": hasattr(b["pipeline"], "steps"),
        "preprocessing inside the pipeline": any("scal" in n or "prep" in n or "impute" in n
                                                 for n, _ in b["pipeline"].steps),
        "feature order recorded":            bool(b.get("feature_names")),
        "library version recorded":          bool(b.get("sklearn_version")),
        "test score recorded":               b.get("test_r2") is not None,
        "training date recorded":            bool(b.get("trained_on")),
        "file is loadable":                  os.path.getsize(bundle_path) > 0,
    }
    for name, ok in checks.items():
        print(f"  {'✓' if ok else '✗'}  {name}")
    return all(checks.values())

print("PRE-FLIGHT CHECKS")
print(f"\nready to deploy: {preflight(bundle_path)}")

PRE-FLIGHT CHECKS
  ✓  pipeline saved (not a bare model)
  ✓  preprocessing inside the pipeline
  ✓  feature order recorded
  ✓  library version recorded
  ✓  test score recorded
  ✓  training date recorded
  ✓  file is loadable

ready to deploy: True




18.1.3 ❓ Check yourself
Q1. You save only the LinearRegression and not its scaler. What happens in production?


The app crashes on the first request.


It returns confident, wrong predictions with no error.


Predictions are slightly less accurate.


Q2. A nightly job scores every customer for churn risk and writes a CSV. What kind of deployment?


Online.


Offline (batch).


Neither.


Q3. Why use @st.cache_resource on the model loader?


It makes predictions more accurate.


Streamlit reruns the whole script on every interaction; without it the model reloads from disk each time.


It is required by Streamlit Cloud.


Q4. Your model’s accuracy has fallen six months after launch, but the code is unchanged. Most likely cause?


The file has corrupted.


Drift — the incoming data or the underlying relationship has changed.


Streamlit updated.


Q5. A user asks the app to value a 9,000 sq ft house. The training data went up to 3,000. What should the app do?


Return the prediction.


Refuse, or return it with a prominent warning that it is outside the model’s range.


Return the maximum training price.








NoteAnswers





A1 — (b). Demo 1 measured the size of the error. Silence is what makes it dangerous.
A2 — (b). No server, no latency requirement — the file is the product.
A3 — (b). Every slider move reruns the script top to bottom.
A4 — (b). Demo 10 shows how to catch it by watching inputs rather than waiting for complaints.
A5 — (b). Session 9’s extrapolation warning, now with a user attached.

title: 15  Session 13 — Big Data Analytics Fundamentals
text:
16.1 1. The five Vs
Big data is usually described with five words beginning with V. They are useful as a checklist, provided you remember that only one of them is usually your actual problem.








V
Means
The problem it creates




Volume
how much there is
it does not fit in memory or on one disk


Velocity
how fast it arrives
you cannot store it before the next batch arrives


Variety
how many shapes it comes in
text, images, JSON and tables need different handling


Veracity
how much you can trust it
sensors fail, users lie, systems disagree


Value
whether it is worth anything
most of it is never used









Tip🧠 Analogy — the library



Volume — the library has ten million books, and no room for shelves. Velocity — twelve thousand new books arrive every hour. Variety — some are books, some are scrolls, some are audio recordings. Veracity — some are unreliable, and some are simply wrong. Value — nine million of them will never be opened.
A library with a volume problem needs a bigger building. One with a velocity problem needs a faster door. They are different problems with different solutions, and calling both “big data” hides that.

title: 15  Session 13 — Big Data Analytics Fundamentals
section: 16.2 2. Where one machine stops being enough
text:
16.2 2. Where one machine stops being enough
The honest threshold is not a number of rows. It is the point where the work no longer fits in memory.
A rough guide: pandas comfortably handles data up to about one fifth of your RAM, because operations make copies. Beyond that your machine starts swapping to disk and everything slows by orders of magnitude.

16.2.1 Demo 1 — measure it on your own machine

import numpy as np, pandas as pd, time

def timed(f):
    t = time.perf_counter(); out = f(); return out, time.perf_counter() - t

# Read one real file, then time the same operation on growing slices of it.
base = pd.read_csv("datasets/transactions.csv", usecols=["shop", "amount"])
big = pd.concat([base] * 20, ignore_index=True)      # 4 million rows from one file
print(f"source file: {len(base):,} rows; stacked to {len(big):,} for the largest test\n")

print(f"{'rows':>12} {'memory':>12} {'groupby time':>14} {'per M rows':>12}")
print("-" * 54)
for n in [10_000, 100_000, 1_000_000, 4_000_000]:
    df = big.iloc[:n]
    mem = df.memory_usage(deep=True).sum() / 1e6
    _, secs = timed(lambda: df.groupby("shop")["amount"].mean())
    print(f"{n:>12,} {mem:>10.1f} MB {secs*1000:>12.1f} ms {secs/(n/1e6)*1000:>10.1f} ms")

print("\nThe cost per million rows stays roughly flat — pandas is not struggling yet.")
print("It struggles when the data plus its working copies stop fitting in RAM.")

source file: 200,000 rows; stacked to 4,000,000 for the largest test

        rows       memory   groupby time   per M rows
------------------------------------------------------
      10,000        0.2 MB          2.6 ms      259.2 ms
     100,000        1.6 MB          1.0 ms       10.1 ms
   1,000,000       16.0 MB          9.6 ms        9.6 ms
   4,000,000       64.0 MB         51.0 ms       12.8 ms

The cost per million rows stays roughly flat — pandas is not struggling yet.
It struggles when the data plus its working copies stop fitting in RAM.




16.2.2 Demo 2 — how much memory a realistic table needs

import numpy as np, pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("datasets/transactions.csv", parse_dates=["ts"])
n = len(df)

per_row = df.memory_usage(deep=True).sum() / n
print(f"this table: {df.memory_usage(deep=True).sum()/1e6:.1f} MB for {n:,} rows "
      f"({per_row:.0f} bytes per row)\n")

print(f"{'rows':>16} {'estimated size':>16} {'fits in 16 GB RAM?'}")
for rows in [1e6, 1e7, 1e8, 1e9]:
    gb = rows * per_row / 1e9
    verdict = "yes, comfortably" if gb < 3 else "tight — use chunks" if gb < 16 else "NO — needs a cluster"
    print(f"{rows:>16,.0f} {gb:>13.1f} GB   {verdict}")

this table: 17.2 MB for 200,000 rows (86 bytes per row)

            rows   estimated size fits in 16 GB RAM?
       1,000,000           0.1 GB   yes, comfortably
      10,000,000           0.9 GB   yes, comfortably
     100,000,000           8.6 GB   tight — use chunks
   1,000,000,000          86.0 GB   NO — needs a cluster




16.2.3 Demo 3 — two ways to survive a file bigger than memory
Before reaching for a cluster, two techniques solve most “too big” problems on one machine.

import numpy as np, pandas as pd, tempfile, os

path = "datasets/transactions.csv"
n = sum(1 for _ in open(path)) - 1
print(f"file on disk: {os.path.getsize(path)/1e6:.1f} MB, {n:,} rows\n")

# --- TECHNIQUE 1: chunking. Never hold the whole file at once. -------------
running_total, running_count = 0.0, 0
per_city = {}
for chunk in pd.read_csv(path, chunksize=50_000):        # 50,000 rows at a time
    running_total += chunk["amount"].sum()
    running_count += len(chunk)
    for city, total in chunk.groupby("city")["amount"].sum().items():
        per_city[city] = per_city.get(city, 0) + total

print(f"CHUNKED: mean amount {running_total/running_count:.2f} over {running_count:,} rows")
print(f"         totals per city: { {k: round(v) for k, v in per_city.items()} }")
print(f"         peak memory held: one chunk of 50,000 rows, not {n:,}")

# --- TECHNIQUE 2: read only what you need ---------------------------------
narrow = pd.read_csv(path, usecols=["city", "amount"])
wide   = pd.read_csv(path)
print(f"\nCOLUMN SELECTION: all columns {wide.memory_usage(deep=True).sum()/1e6:.1f} MB")
print(f"                  two columns  {narrow.memory_usage(deep=True).sum()/1e6:.1f} MB")

# --- BONUS: the right dtype often halves the memory -----------------------
compact = wide.copy()
compact["city"] = compact["city"].astype("category")
compact["shop"] = compact["shop"].astype("int8")
print(f"\nDTYPES:  before {wide.memory_usage(deep=True).sum()/1e6:.1f} MB"
      f"  →  after {compact.memory_usage(deep=True).sum()/1e6:.1f} MB")

file on disk: 7.1 MB, 200,000 rows

CHUNKED: mean amount 500.32 over 200,000 rows
         totals per city: {'Delhi': 33243295, 'Mumbai': 33508355, 'Pune': 33311979}
         peak memory held: one chunk of 50,000 rows, not 200,000

COLUMN SELECTION: all columns 30.8 MB
                  two columns  14.0 MB

DTYPES:  before 30.8 MB  →  after 17.2 MB








Warning⚠️ Try these before you build a cluster



Chunking, selecting columns and fixing dtypes routinely turn a “we need Spark” problem back into a laptop problem. A distributed cluster costs money, expertise and debugging time. Spend a day on the three techniques above first — most of the time, that is the whole solution.

text:
17.1 3. The four questions
Every analysis is one of four kinds, in increasing order of difficulty and value.









Type
Question
Example
Covered in




Descriptive
What happened?
sales fell 12% last quarter
Sessions 7–8


Diagnostic
Why did it happen?
the fall was entirely in one region
Session 8


Predictive
What will happen?
next quarter will fall another 5%
Sessions 9–11


Prescriptive
What should we do?
move stock to the region that is growing
Session 16








flowchart LR
    D["<b>Descriptive</b><br/>what happened?"] --> G["<b>Diagnostic</b><br/>why?"]
    G --> P["<b>Predictive</b><br/>what next?"]
    P --> X["<b>Prescriptive</b><br/>what should we do?"]







17.1.1 Demo 4 — all four on one dataset

import numpy as np, pandas as pd

sales = pd.read_csv("datasets/regional_sales.csv", parse_dates=["month"])

# 1. DESCRIPTIVE — what happened?
by_month = sales.groupby("month")["sales"].sum()
change = (by_month.iloc[-1] - by_month.iloc[0]) / by_month.iloc[0]
print(f"DESCRIPTIVE : total sales moved {change:+.1%} across the year")

# 2. DIAGNOSTIC — why?
by_region = sales.groupby("region").apply(
    lambda g: (g.sort_values("month")["sales"].iloc[-1] -
               g.sort_values("month")["sales"].iloc[0]), include_groups=False)
print("DIAGNOSTIC  : change by region over the year")
for r, v in by_region.items():
    print(f"                {r:<6} {v:>+10,.0f}")
print(f"              → the decline is entirely {by_region.idxmin()}; the others grew")

# 3. PREDICTIVE — what next?
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
x = np.arange(len(by_month)).reshape(-1, 1)
trend_model = LinearRegression().fit(x, by_month.values)
next3 = trend_model.predict([[12], [13], [14]])
print(f"PREDICTIVE  : next three months ≈ {', '.join(f'{v:,.0f}' for v in next3)}")

# 4. PRESCRIPTIVE — what should we do?
growing = by_region[by_region > 0].index.tolist()
print(f"PRESCRIPTIVE: shift investment from {by_region.idxmin()} to {', '.join(growing)};")
print(f"              re-examine {by_region.idxmin()} before writing it off")

DESCRIPTIVE : total sales moved -0.6% across the year
DIAGNOSTIC  : change by region over the year
                North      -9,451
                South      +4,045
                West       +4,639
              → the decline is entirely North; the others grew
PREDICTIVE  : next three months ≈ 120,147, 120,128, 120,110
PRESCRIPTIVE: shift investment from North to South, West;
              re-examine North before writing it off


Notice the increasing difficulty. Descriptive is a groupby. Prescriptive needs a prediction and a judgement about what to do with it — which is why the last one is never fully automatic.

title: 15  Session 13 — Big Data Analytics Fundamentals
text:
18.1 4. How HDFS works
HDFS — the Hadoop Distributed File System — stores one enormous file across many ordinary machines, and keeps working when some of them fail.
Three ideas do all the work:







Idea
What it means




Blocks
the file is cut into fixed-size pieces, typically 128 MB


Replication
every block is stored on three different machines


Write once
files are appended to, never edited in the middle








flowchart TB
    F["one 400 MB file"] --> B1["block 1<br/>128 MB"]
    F --> B2["block 2<br/>128 MB"]
    F --> B3["block 3<br/>128 MB"]
    F --> B4["block 4<br/>16 MB"]
    B1 --> N["<b>NameNode</b><br/>remembers which block<br/>is on which machine"]
    B2 --> N
    B3 --> N
    B4 --> N
    N --> D1["DataNode 1"]
    N --> D2["DataNode 2"]
    N --> D3["DataNode 3"]






The NameNode holds the index — which blocks make up which file, and where each copy lives. The DataNodes hold the actual blocks. The NameNode never touches the data itself, which is why one modest machine can index petabytes.

18.1.1 Demo 5 — block splitting and replication, simulated

import math

def plan_storage(file_gb, block_mb=128, replication=3, datanodes=6):
    blocks = math.ceil(file_gb * 1024 / block_mb)
    copies = blocks * replication
    print(f"file size        : {file_gb} GB")
    print(f"block size       : {block_mb} MB")
    print(f"blocks           : {blocks:,}")
    print(f"copies stored    : {blocks:,} × {replication} = {copies:,}")
    print(f"disk used        : {file_gb * replication} GB "
          f"({replication}× the file, the price of surviving failures)")
    print(f"blocks per node  : about {copies // datanodes:,} across {datanodes} machines")
    print(f"machines that can fail without data loss: {replication - 1}")

plan_storage(400)

file size        : 400 GB
block size       : 128 MB
blocks           : 3,200
copies stored    : 3,200 × 3 = 9,600
disk used        : 1200 GB (3× the file, the price of surviving failures)
blocks per node  : about 1,600 across 6 machines
machines that can fail without data loss: 2




18.1.2 Demo 6 — why replication is worth 3× the disk

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(75)
n_nodes, annual_failure_rate, trials = 200, 0.04, 20_000

for replication in [1, 2, 3]:
    lost = 0
    for _ in range(trials):
        failed = rng.random(n_nodes) < annual_failure_rate
        # a block is lost only if every machine holding a copy fails
        holders = rng.choice(n_nodes, replication, replace=False)
        if failed[holders].all():
            lost += 1
    print(f"replication {replication}: chance a given block is lost in a year "
          f"= {lost/trials:.4%}")

print(f"\n(with {n_nodes} machines and a {annual_failure_rate:.0%} annual failure rate)")
print("Three copies turns near-certain annual data loss into a negligible risk.")

replication 1: chance a given block is lost in a year = 4.2350%
replication 2: chance a given block is lost in a year = 0.1050%
replication 3: chance a given block is lost in a year = 0.0100%

(with 200 machines and a 4% annual failure rate)
Three copies turns near-certain annual data loss into a negligible risk.

title: 15  Session 13 — Big Data Analytics Fundamentals
text:
18.2 5. Talking to HDFS
HDFS commands look deliberately like ordinary shell commands. These need a running Hadoop cluster, so they are shown rather than executed here.
# List a directory in the cluster
hdfs dfs -ls /user/data/logs
# Found 1 items
# -rw-r--r--   3 hadoop supergroup  1099511627776 2024-01-01 12:00 /user/data/logs/clicks.csv
#              ↑
#        this 3 is the replication factor: every block exists on three machines

# Copy a local file INTO the cluster
hdfs dfs -put ./local_logs.csv /user/data/logs/

# Copy a file back OUT of the cluster
hdfs dfs -get /user/data/logs/clicks.csv ./downloaded.csv

# Peek at the first lines of a 1 TB file, without downloading it
hdfs dfs -cat /user/data/logs/clicks.csv | head -20

# How is this file actually laid out across the cluster?
hdfs fsck /user/data/logs/clicks.csv -files -blocks -locations






Important🔓 Running this yourself



You do not need a cluster to complete this course. Three options, easiest first:








Option
What you get
Effort




PySpark local mode
everything in Session 14 except the hdfs dfs commands
pip install pyspark, needs Java 17


Docker
a real single-node Hadoop, so hdfs dfs commands work
one docker run


A hosted sandbox
a full cluster in a browser
sign-up only



Every executable cell in this chapter and the next runs in local mode. The bash blocks above are reference — they are the commands you would type against a real cluster.








Warning⚠️ HDFS is terrible at small files



One 128 MB file uses one block and one entry in the NameNode’s index. A million 128-byte files use a million entries — and the NameNode keeps its index in memory. Small files exhaust the cluster’s index long before they exhaust its disks.
The fix is always the same: combine small files into large ones before storing them.



def namenode_pressure(total_gb, avg_file_mb):
    files = total_gb * 1024 / avg_file_mb
    # roughly 150 bytes of NameNode memory per file plus per block
    mem_gb = files * 150 * 2 / 1e9
    print(f"{total_gb:>6} GB as {avg_file_mb:>6.2f} MB files → {files:>12,.0f} files, "
          f"NameNode index ≈ {mem_gb:>7.2f} GB")

print("Same amount of data, different file sizes:")
for size in [256, 64, 1, 0.1]:
    namenode_pressure(10_000, size)

Same amount of data, different file sizes:
 10000 GB as 256.00 MB files →       40,000 files, NameNode index ≈    0.01 GB
 10000 GB as  64.00 MB files →      160,000 files, NameNode index ≈    0.05 GB
 10000 GB as   1.00 MB files →   10,240,000 files, NameNode index ≈    3.07 GB
 10000 GB as   0.10 MB files →  102,400,000 files, NameNode index ≈   30.72 GB

section: 19.2 7. When not to use any of this
text:
19.2 7. When not to use any of this
Distributed tools have a fixed overhead. Below a certain size they are slower than pandas, not faster.

19.2.1 Demo 7 — the overhead, quantified

import numpy as np, pandas as pd, time

CLUSTER_STARTUP_S = 8.0        # a real Spark session takes seconds to start
PER_TASK_OVERHEAD = 0.15       # scheduling, serialising, shuffling

base = pd.read_csv("datasets/transactions.csv", usecols=["shop", "amount"])
big = pd.concat([base] * 25, ignore_index=True)

print(f"{'rows':>12} {'pandas':>10} {'distributed (modelled)':>24}   winner")
print("-" * 62)
for n in [10_000, 100_000, 1_000_000, 5_000_000]:
    df = big.iloc[:n]

    t = time.perf_counter()
    df.groupby("shop")["amount"].mean()
    pandas_s = time.perf_counter() - t

    # A cluster splits the work but pays startup and coordination costs.
    partitions = max(4, n // 250_000)
    dist_s = CLUSTER_STARTUP_S + PER_TASK_OVERHEAD * partitions + (pandas_s / 8)

    winner = "pandas" if pandas_s < dist_s else "distributed"
    print(f"{n:>12,} {pandas_s*1000:>8.1f} ms {dist_s*1000:>21,.0f} ms   {winner}")

print("\nThe modelled cluster never wins here, because none of these datasets is")
print("large enough to repay an 8-second startup. That crossover is the number")
print("you must find for yourself — Session 14 measures it with real Spark.")

        rows     pandas   distributed (modelled)   winner
--------------------------------------------------------------
      10,000      0.6 ms                 8,600 ms   pandas
     100,000      1.1 ms                 8,600 ms   pandas
   1,000,000     12.2 ms                 8,602 ms   pandas
   5,000,000     65.2 ms                11,008 ms   pandas

The modelled cluster never wins here, because none of these datasets is
large enough to repay an 8-second startup. That crossover is the number
you must find for yourself — Session 14 measures it with real Spark.








Warning⚠️ ‘Big data’ is a claim that needs evidence



Before adopting distributed tooling, answer three questions with numbers:

How large is the data actually? — in GB, measured, not estimated
Have I tried chunking, column selection and dtypes? — Demo 3
How long does the job take now, and how long is acceptable?

If the answer to 3 is “four minutes, and ten would be fine”, you do not have a big-data problem. You have a four-minute job.




19.2.2 ❓ Check yourself
Q1. A hospital receives 50,000 sensor readings per second and must react within a second. Which V is the problem?


Volume.


Velocity.


Value.


Q2. A 40 GB CSV must be summarised on a laptop with 16 GB of RAM. What do you try first?


Buy a cluster.


Read it in chunks and select only the needed columns.


Sample 1% and hope.


Q3. “Sales fell because the North region lost its two largest customers.” Which type?


Descriptive.


Diagnostic.


Prescriptive.


Q4. HDFS replicates every block three times. What does that cost and buy?


Costs nothing, buys speed.


Costs 3× the disk, buys survival when up to two machines holding a block fail.


Costs 3× the time, buys accuracy.


Q5. Your cluster has plenty of disk free but the NameNode is out of memory. Likely cause?


A single enormous file.


Millions of tiny files, each needing an index entry.


Replication set too low.








NoteAnswers





A1 — (b). The total volume may be modest; the difficulty is the rate and the deadline.
A2 — (b). Demo 3. Chunking plus column selection solves most of these.
A3 — (b). It explains why, which is the diagnostic question.
A4 — (b). Demo 6 measured the failure probabilities.
A5 — (b). The small-files problem — the NameNode’s index lives in memory.
